units.notes:
Management = “the art of getting things done through the efforts of other people”. The book's key-term version: creatively solving problems to accomplish organizational goals through the efforts of others.

The P-O-L-C framework (the four functions)

FunctionWhat it meansIncludes
PlanningSetting objectives and deciding the course of action to reach them. Needs environmental scanning, forecasting and good decisions.Vision & mission, strategizing, goals & objectives
OrganizingDeveloping an organizational structure and allocating human resources so objectives are reached. Also job design.Organization design, culture, social networks
LeadingThe social and informal sources of influence you use to inspire action by others.Leadership, decision making, communication, teams, motivation
ControllingMaking sure performance doesn't deviate from standards. Three steps: (1) set performance standards, (2) compare actual performance with the standards, (3) take corrective action when needed.Systems & processes, strategic HR

Three levels of planning

LevelTimeWhoWhat
Strategic3+ yearsTop managementWhole organization, mission-driven, competitive positioning (based on SWOT)
Tactical1–3 yearsMiddle managersConcrete means to implement the strategic plan
OperationalUnder 1 yearLower managersSpecific action steps that support the strategic and tactical plans

Leadership, entrepreneurship and strategy

Leadership: an act of influence that inspires action by others; the social and informal sources of influence.

Entrepreneurship: recognizing opportunities (needs, wants, problems) and using or creating resources to implement innovative ideas for new ventures. An intrapreneur does this inside an existing organization.

Strategy: the central, integrated, externally oriented concept of how an organization will achieve its objectives (Hambrick & Fredrickson).

Performance

Triple bottom line: performance on economic, social and environmental dimensions (profit, people, planet). Linked to CSR: taking responsibility for your impact on customers, employees, communities and the environment beyond what the law requires.

In-role performance: the productivity and quality your job requires. OCB (organizational citizenship behaviour): voluntary, extra-role behaviour that helps the organization.

Group performance = the inputs of the group minus process loss (anything in group interaction that hurts problem solving).

Traditional vs contemporary view

Traditional: a top-down pyramid. Contemporary: an upside-down pyramid where top managers support and serve other managers and employees (empowerment), who serve the customers. Today's trends: DEI and sustainability.

units.notes:
Personality: a person's relatively stable feelings, thoughts and behavioural patterns. Stable, but it can change slowly over a lifetime. Behaviour at work also depends on what the job expects; personality matters most in jobs with a lot of autonomy.

The Big Five (OCEAN)

TraitDescriptionAt work
OpennessCurious, original, intellectual, creative, open to new ideasLearns fast, adapts to change, creative; may get bored by routine
ConscientiousnessOrganized, systematic, punctual, achievement-oriented, dependableThe one trait that predicts performance across all jobs; most wanted by recruiters
ExtraversionOutgoing, talkative, sociableGood in sales and as managers; more absenteeism
AgreeablenessAffable, tolerant, sensitive, trusting, kind, warmHelps others; avoids conflict, so less change-oriented communication
NeuroticismAnxious, irritable, temperamental, moodyThe only trait where high is undesirable; unhappy, lower career success

Other personality dimensions

Self-monitoring: how well you read a situation and adjust your behaviour (“social chameleons”).

Proactive personality: inclination to fix what is wrong and take initiative without being told.

Self-esteem: overall positive feelings about yourself.

Self-efficacy: belief that you can perform a specific task successfully. Task-specific, unlike the other traits.

Personality tests in selection

Controversial: candidates can fake answers, and personality explains only about 10–15% of job performance. Cognitive ability (general mental ability) predicts performance better. Tests must not discriminate.

Values

Values: people's stable life goals, what matters most to them. They affect job choice and whether people stay. Schwartz's 10 values: achievement, benevolence, conformity, hedonism, power, security, self-direction, stimulation, tradition, universalism.

units.notes:
An attitude = our opinions, beliefs and feelings about aspects of our environment. Two work attitudes matter most:

Job satisfaction: the feelings people have toward their job. Probably the most studied attitude.

Organizational commitment: the emotional attachment to the company. A committed employee believes in its values, puts in effort and wants to stay (“we have great benefits”).

What causes positive work attitudes

FactorDetail
Personality & valuese.g. low neuroticism → more satisfied
Job characteristicsSkill variety, autonomy, feedback, significant tasks. Matters most for people with a high need for growth.
Organizational justiceDistributive (fair pay and rewards), procedural (fair policies and processes), interactional (treated with dignity and respect). At its root: trust.
Psychological contractThe unspoken understanding of what the employee gives (effort, loyalty) and gets (pay, raises, job security)
Relationships at workWith coworkers and especially the manager. Relationship management = communicating clearly, keeping good relationships, managing conflict.
StressEnvironmental, interpersonal, organizational stressors. Role ambiguity = unclear responsibilities; role conflict = contradictory demands. More stress → less satisfaction (but challenging stress can be positive).

Measuring attitudes

Attitude surveys (work best when confidential and followed by action) and exit interviews with departing employees.

Attitudes predict intentions better than actual behaviour: a dissatisfied employee intends to leave, but whether they leave depends on alternatives.

The interactionist perspective: fit

Behaviour is a function of the person and the situation interacting.

Person-job fit: your knowledge, skills, abilities and other characteristics (KSAO) match the job demands.

Person-organization fit: your personality, values and goals match the organization.

Good fit → more satisfied, more committed, stay longer.

Case: SAS Institute
On Fortune's best places to work every year; turnover under 4% where 20% is the industry norm. Google visited the SAS campus for ideas.

Values match the company = person-organization fit. Skills match the job = person-job fit.

units.notes:
Leadership = the act of influencing others to work toward a goal. Leaders exist at every level.

Formal leaders hold a position of authority and can use their position power as well as personal power.

Informal leaders have no formal position but influence others through personal power. The group acknowledges them.

Designated leader: put in the role by outside forces. Emergent leader: arises from the group's dynamics while working toward a goal.

The leadership process (Hollander & Julian): a complex, dynamic exchange relationship built over time between leader and followers who depend on each other to reach a shared goal.

French & Raven: five sources of power

PowerBased onType
LegitimateThe formal position or title: the “right” to give instructionsPosition
RewardAbility to give rewards (bonuses, promotions, good territories)Position
CoerciveAbility to punish or take away something valuedPosition
ExpertKnowledge and skills others needPersonal
ReferentOthers admire the person and want to be associated with themPersonal

Effects: coercive power alienates followers. Reward power makes people think “how much am I getting?”. Referent power creates identification with the leader. Expert power and rational arguments create commitment. Referent and expert power give the best satisfaction and performance; referent power strengthens all the other powers.

Influence-based leadership styles

Tannenbaum & Schmidt continuum: from boss-centred (autocratic) to participative to free-rein.

McGregor's Theory X leader: assumes people dislike work → controlling style. Theory Y leader: assumes people are creative and self-directed → involving style.

Muczyk & Reimann: directive autocrat, permissive autocrat, directive democrat, permissive democrat (shares decisions and execution).

Who is a leader? Trait approaches

Started with Stogdill: what physical, personality and social traits make leaders? Kirkpatrick & Locke found core traits that give leadership potential:

Drive · leadership motivation · honesty and integrity · self-confidence · cognitive ability · knowledge of the business · (charisma, creativity, flexibility).

Traits related to leadership (Judge et al.):

TraitFinding

Limitation: traits matter more in small, flexible firms than in rule-bound ones, and the situation is ignored. Leaders are not simply “born”.

units.notes:
Transformational vs transactional

TransformationalTransactional
Aligns employee goals with the leader's and company's goals; followers start caring about the company's well-beingGets the right behaviour by giving resources and rewards in exchange
Four tools: charisma · inspirational motivation (inspiring vision) · intellectual stimulation (challenge the status quo, think creatively) · individualized consideration (personal care)Three methods: contingent rewards (reward for accomplishments) · active management by exception (prevent problems before they happen) · passive management by exception (wait until something goes wrong)
Builds trust; strongest effect on effectiveness and satisfactionAlso effective, except passive management by exception

Best: show both. Charisma can be trained, isn't required, and has a dark side (Enron's Skilling).

Charismatic leadership

Charisma: a leader's charm and magnetism that inspires confidence, commitment and admiration. Leaders of social movements rely on charisma rather than authority.

Servant leadership

The leader's role is to serve the needs of others: develop employees, help them reach their goals, serve the community. Focus on ethics and self-sacrifice (Greenleaf; Abraham Lincoln).

Authentic leadership

Key advice: “be yourself”. Authentic leaders are self-aware, act consistently with their values and draw strength from their own life experiences (Howard Schultz at Starbucks gave health insurance to part-timers because of his father's experience).

Leader-member exchange (LMX)

High-quality LMX: trust, liking, respect; both go beyond the job description (in-group). Low-quality LMX: just the formal job (out-group).

units.notes:
Communication: a process by which information is exchanged between individuals through a common system of symbols, signs or behaviour. Managers spend 50–90% of their time communicating.

Three functions in an organization: transmitting information · coordinating effort · sharing emotions and feelings.

The communication process

Sender has an idea and encodes it (turns it into words, diagrams, numbers) → the message travels through a channel/medium (oral, written, nonverbal) → the receiver decodes it (gives it meaning) → feedback back to the sender. Noise = anything that distorts the message (in the environment, the receiver or the sender).

Barriers to effective communication

BarrierMeaning
FilteringDistorting or withholding information to manage someone's reaction
Selective perceptionFiltering what you see and hear to fit your own needs and beliefs
Information overloadReceiving more information than you can take in
Emotional disconnectsSender or receiver is upset, so the message is ignored or distorted
Lack of source familiarity or credibilityNo shared context, or an untrustworthy sender
Workplace gossip (grapevine)Unofficial information that may not be accurate
Semantics / differences in meaningWords mean different things to different people (age, culture, jargon)
Gender differencesDifferent communication styles
Biased languageWords that stereotype, offend or exclude

Listening: workers listen 55% of the time, leaders up to 70%. Active listening: full attention, no interrupting, reflecting and asking questions.

Types and channels

TypeExamples
Verbal (oral)Phone, video calls, meetings, in person. Better for feelings.
WrittenMemos, e-mails, texts, letters, manuals, policies. Better for facts.
NonverbalFacial expressions, body stance, tone of voice. About 55% of in-person communication; only 7% comes from the words.

Information richness: face-to-face, phone and video are richest; e-mail, blogs and memos are medium; formal documents and spreadsheets are leanest.

Direction: downward (from leaders), upward (from the front line), horizontal/lateral (between peers), diagonal (across levels and departments).

Facial expressions = nonverbal; a phone call is verbal; a memo or text is written (mock Q11).

units.notes:
Decision making: making choices among alternative courses of action, including inaction. About half of leaders' decisions fail.

Types of decisions

By how often
ProgrammedOccur often enough to have an automated response (a decision rule). E.g. automatic reorder at a stock level.
NonprogrammedUnique and important: conscious thinking, information gathering, careful consideration. E.g. a crisis, McDonald's dropping trans fats.
By organizational level
StrategicLong term, set the course of the organization
TacticalHow things will get done (mid-term action plans)
OperationalDaily decisions employees make to run the organization

Four decision-making models

ModelDefinitionUse when
RationalStructured, logical steps to choose the optimal alternativeInformation can be quantified, the decision is important, you want to maximize the outcome
Bounded rationalityLimited information, time and brainpower → satisfice: take the first alternative that meets the minimum criteriaMinimum criteria are clear, little time, not maximizing
IntuitiveGut feeling, experience, pattern recognition, fastGoals unclear, time pressure, you have experience
CreativeLess structured, generates novel solutionsNo clear solution, new ideas needed, you have time

Rational steps: identify the problem → set criteria → weight criteria → generate all alternatives → evaluate them → choose the best → implement → evaluate the decision.

Creative steps: problem identification → immersion (gather information) → incubation (set it aside; unconscious work) → illumination (insight moment) → verification and application. Creativity is judged on fluency (number of ideas), flexibility (variety) and originality.

Faulty decisions

Overconfidence bias (overestimating your abilities) · hindsight bias (mistakes look obvious afterwards) · anchoring (relying too much on one piece of information) · framing bias (influenced by how it's presented) · escalation of commitment (continuing a failing course because you already invested) · analysis paralysis.

Individual vs group decisions

Groups: more experiences and perspectives, more creative, easier implementation, but slower, coordination problems, rarely beat their best member. Problems: groupthink (avoiding critical evaluation of ideas the group favours; members stay silent to keep agreement; Challenger launch) and social loafing (some members put in less effort).

Techniques: Nominal Group Technique (write ideas alone → share → discuss → vote) · Delphi (written questionnaires, no meeting, until consensus) · majority rule · consensus (everyone agrees) · brainstorming (no criticism, wild ideas, build on others) · GDSS (computer systems) · decision trees.

Stakeholders

3. Strategy implementationDoing it: training, allocating resources

units.t: How strategies emerge: intended vs realized
units.notes:
StrategyMeaning
IntendedConceived by the top management team, through negotiation, bargaining and compromise
DeliberateThe part of the intended strategy that is actually carried out (design school: rational, top-down planning)
UnrealizedThe parts of the plan that never happen
EmergentDecisions that emerge as leaders interpret the plan and adapt to changing circumstances; often bottom-up (emergence or learning school)
RealizedWhat is actually implemented = deliberate + emergent

Mintzberg: only 10–30% of intended strategy is realized. Why plans fail: poorly built plan, competitors undermine it, or poor execution.

The more volatile the environment, the more emergence. Stable organizations (postal services) can plan in detail. Book example: Intel's switch from memory chips to microprocessors grew from plant-level decisions.

Best practice: balance design (planning) with the flexibility to benefit from emergence. Headquarters sets mission, targets and budgets; units adapt and experiment.

Exam trap
“Pilot results led to a different approach than the original plan” = emergent strategy that became the realized strategy (mock Q33).

units.t: Goals, MBO, Balanced Scorecard, SMART, KPI, CSR
units.notes:
Goals: outcome statements that define what the organization is trying to accomplish. Objectives: very precise, time-based, measurable actions that support a goal (linked to SMART).

Planning starts with vision and mission → strategy → goals and objectives show whether you're on track. Horizons: long term 3+ years, mid-range 1–3 years, short term under 1 year.

Tools

ToolWhat it is
Management by Objectives (MBO)Drucker (1954). Systematic approach that aligns subordinates' objectives with the overall goals; employees help set their own objectives and timelines.
Balanced ScorecardKaplan & Norton. Translates mission, vision and strategy into specific, measurable goals and monitors them in four areas: financial, customer, internal business processes, learning & growth. Financial + non-financial; leading and lagging measures.
SMARTSpecific, Measurable, Achievable, Realistic, Time-bound
KPIA measurable value that shows how effectively a company achieves key business objectives

CSR and the triple bottom line

CSR: how companies manage their business processes to produce an overall positive effect on society. The Balanced Scorecard can help make CSR values measurable (Crawford & Scaletta).

Triple bottom line: measuring performance on social, environmental and economic dimensions (people, planet, profit).

Examples in the slides: Dow Jones Sustainability Index (DJSI), UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) for 2030, Net Zero targets.
units.trap:
Exam traps
“An outcome statement of what to accomplish” = goal. “Precise, time-based, measurable action” = objective (mock Q16, Q17).
Balanced Scorecard = turns mission and strategy into measurable goals and tracks them (mock Q18), not “only financial targets”.
terms: Outcome statements that define what an organization is trying to accomplish.
Precise, time-based, measurable actions that support a goal.
Management by Objectives: aligning subordinate objectives with organizational goals (Drucker).
Translates mission and strategy into measurable goals in four perspectives.
Measurable value showing how effectively key objectives are achieved.
Managing business processes to produce an overall positive effect on society.
Performance on social, environmental and economic dimensions.

units.notes:
Motivation: “the intention of achieving a goal, leading to goal-directed behaviour”.

Performance = Motivation × Ability × Environment

Need-based theories

TheoryCore idea
MaslowFive needs in a hierarchy: physiological → safety → social → esteem → self-actualization. A satisfied need no longer motivates.
ERG (Alderfer)Three groups: Existence (= physiological + safety), Relatedness (= social), Growth (= esteem + self-actualization). No fixed order, several needs at once, frustration-regression.
Herzberg two-factorHygiene factors (company policies, supervision, working conditions, salary, safety, security) prevent dissatisfaction but don't motivate. Motivators (achievement, recognition, interesting work, responsibility, advancement, growth) really motivate.
McClellandAcquired needs: achievement, affiliation, power

Process-based theories

TheoryCore idea
Equity theory (Adams)We compare our inputs (effort, loyalty, skills) and outputs (pay, rewards) with a referent. Inequity creates tension → we reduce our own input, ask for more, distort perceptions, change referent or leave.
Expectancy theoryExpectancy (effort → performance), instrumentality (performance → reward), valence (value of the reward)
Goal-setting theory (Locke & Latham)Supported in 1,000+ studies. SMART goals give direction, energize, challenge and push creative thinking. Downsides: tunnel vision, ignoring unmeasured work, unethical behaviour.
Reinforcement theoryPositive and negative reinforcement increase behaviour; extinction and punishment reduce it

Justice beyond equity: distributive (fair outcomes), procedural (fair process), interactional (respectful treatment).
units.trap:
Exam traps
Better office temperature, job security or clear policies = hygiene. Meaningful responsibility for complete projects = motivator (mock Q14).
She sees a colleague get the same reward for less effort and cuts her own effort = equity theory (mock Q15).
terms: The intention of achieving a goal, leading to goal-directed behaviour.
Existence, relatedness, growth; several needs at once; frustration-regression.
Job context factors that cause dissatisfaction when missing (pay, policies, conditions).
Intrinsic job factors that truly motivate (achievement, recognition, responsibility).
Motivation from fairness, comparing input/output ratios with a referent.
The person or group you compare yourself with.
Belief that effort will lead to the desired outcome.

units.notes:
Internal and external environments

External (macro, general) environment: the big-picture world with political, economic, social, technological, environmental and legal factors the company barely controls. Tools: PESTEL (macro forces), Porter's 5 forces (competitors).

Internal environment: resources, capabilities and activities. Tools: VRIO, value chain.

Slide examples: 2025 US tariffs and the impact of AI changing internal structures and business activities.

Mechanistic vs organic

Mechanistic: top-down hierarchy, rules, centralized, narrow span of control. For stable, simple environments.

Organic: flatter, participative, fewer rules, wider span of control. For unstable, complex environments.

Six structures

StructureOrganized byPlus / minus
FunctionalDepartments of expertise (R&D, production, finance, HR)+ specialization, economies of scale · − silos, slow coordination
DivisionalDivisions (product, market), each with its own marketing, sales, finance…+ focus, faster customer contact · − duplication, divisions isolated
GeographicLocations of customers (regions, countries)+ local knowledge · − too decentralized
MatrixTwo dimensions: employees report to a functional boss and a project/product boss+ flexibility, cross-functional · − two bosses, confusion, conflict
Network / teamInformal, flexible horizontal teams+ fast, adaptive · − unclear communication, tech-dependent
VirtualBoundaryless, depends on ICT; HQ may be the only fixed base (Uber, Airbnb)+ cost savings, wide talent pool · − isolation, less trust
units.trap:
Exam traps
Engineers stay in their specialist department but also report to product managers = matrix (mock Q28).
Remote specialists across countries working online = virtual. Regional authority = geographic.
terms: The big-picture world of PESTEL factors the organization barely controls.
Top-down, rule-based, centralized; for stable environments.
Flat, flexible, participative; for changing environments.
Organized by departments and areas of expertise.
Functional departments grouped under division heads, each with its own functions.
Organized by the locations of customers.
Employees report to a functional boss and a project/product boss.
Boundaryless organization relying on information and communication technology.

units.notes:
Organizational culture: a system of shared assumptions, values and beliefs that show people what is appropriate and inappropriate behaviour. A rare, hard-to-imitate culture can be a competitive advantage (Barney). Like water to a fish: invisible but shaping behaviour.

Schein's three levels

LevelWhatExample
Artifacts (surface)Visible, tangible aspectsOpen-door policy, office layout, pool tables, company picnics
ValuesShared principles, standards, goalsEgalitarianism, having fun
Assumptions (deepest)Taken for granted, below awareness“Happy employees benefit the organization”

Dimensions of culture

Innovative · aggressive (competitive) · outcome-oriented · stable (predictable, rule-based) · people-oriented (fair, supportive) · team-oriented · detail-oriented.

Strong culture: most employees share the values. An asset or a liability; hard to change; can clash in mergers (Daimler-Chrysler). Subcultures form in departments or locations; a counterculture opposes the main culture.

How culture is created and maintained

Founder values · industry demands · attraction-selection-attrition · onboarding of new employees · leadership · reward systems.

Signs of culture

Mission statement · rituals · rules and policies · physical layout · stories and language.

Diversity

Broad meaning: also personality, cognitive style, education, social background. Advantages: enhances creativity, enhances image, improves outreach to new markets, improves morale. BCG: diversity builds resilience and adaptiveness.

Gender: women earn more degrees but face the glass ceiling (invisible barrier based on prejudice), the pay gap and sexual harassment (quid pro quo, hostile environment; “Me too”).

Sexual orientation and gender identity: sexual minorities have higher education levels on average but still face hiring and treatment discrimination.
units.trap:
Exam traps
The office layout is an artifact (and a sign of culture), not a value.
“Most employees agree on the values” = strong culture. A department opposing the company's values = counterculture.
terms: Shared assumptions, values and beliefs that show what behaviour is appropriate.
Taken-for-granted beliefs at the deepest level of culture.
Most employees agree on the company's values.
Culture within a department, branch or location.
Group whose values oppose the overall culture.
Repetitive activities that teach values and build identification.
How new employees learn the attitudes, knowledge and behaviours they need.
Invisible barrier based on prejudice that stops women advancing.

units.notes:
Hofstede (Dutch social psychologist): culture is “the collective programming of the mind which distinguishes the members of one group or category of people from another”. Survey of 88,000+ IBM employees in 72 countries, four dimensions:

DimensionMeaningHigh / low examples
Power distanceDegree to which members accept differences in power and authorityHigh: Mexico, India, Brazil, China · Low: US, UK, Denmark
Individualism / collectivismFocus on the individual vs on the group as a wholeIndividualist: US, UK, Canada · More collectivist: Asia, Latin America
Uncertainty avoidanceDegree to which people are comfortable with risk, uncertainty and unpredictable situations (high = want clear rules)High: France, Greece, Japan · Low: Denmark, US, UK
MasculinityEmphasis on traditional masculine qualities: achievement, advancement, earnings; clear gender rolesHigh: Japan, Mexico, Germany · Low: Denmark, Finland

High power distance → leaders show authority, subordinates expect clear directions. Collectivist → group-based hiring and decisions, consensus.

GLOBE framework (1990s)

Global Leadership and Organizational Behavior Effectiveness: 170 researchers, 17,000 managers, 62 countries. Nine dimensions; most overlap with Hofstede (uncertainty avoidance, power distance, future orientation, assertiveness, gender egalitarianism, institutional and societal collectivism). Unique to GLOBE: performance orientation (emphasis on performance and achievement) and humane orientation (fairness, altruism, caring).

Countries grouped in clusters (Anglo, Confucian Asia, Germanic Europe, Nordic Europe, Latin America, Middle East, Sub-Saharan Africa) with preferred leadership styles (charismatic, team-oriented, participative, humane-oriented, autonomous, self-protective).

Psychic distance: differences between countries in language, culture, institutions and business practices.
units.trap:
Exam traps
Uncertainty avoidance = comfort with risk and ambiguity, not long-term planning (mock Q21).
Power distance = acceptance of power and authority differences (mock Q22).
Hofstede = 1960s, four dimensions. GLOBE = 1990s, adds performance and humane orientation.
terms: The collective programming of the mind that distinguishes one group from another.
Degree to which a society accepts differences in power and authority.
Focus on the individual's relationship to the group.
Focus on the group as a whole.
Degree to which people are comfortable with risk, uncertainty and unpredictability.

GLOBE: emphasis on performance and achievement.
GLOBE: importance of fairness, altruism and caring.

units.notes:
Globalization: countries becoming more interconnected while trade barriers disappear. That's why international leadership matters.

Three globalization factors

FactorMeaning
Lowering trade barriersTrade agreements and policies remove cross-border barriers such as tariffs (taxes on imports)
Foreign direct investment (FDI)A company invests in another country through ownership positions there (global FDI 2017: $1.52 trillion)
The InternetAny company can sell to anyone in the world; social media builds relationships worldwide

Strategies for expanding globally

StrategyMeaning
GlobalAssumes the world is interconnected and consumption is fairly homogeneous: the same product everywhere
RegionalOrganizes activities (marketing, finance) around key geographic regions (Toyota)
LocalAdapts products to the local market's needs and values

How to go international

Entry modeMeaning
ExportingSelling products made at home abroad. Easiest; exporters are about 17% more profitable.
LicensingFor a royalty or fee, another company may use your trademark, know-how or technology
FranchisingLicensing the whole business model (trademark, structure, training)
Strategic allianceTwo or more companies from different countries agree to do business together; a joint venture creates a new business they own together. Preferred in emerging markets.
FDIFully investing in the host country by building facilities there (e.g. a wholly owned subsidiary)

Exam trap

Investing in another country through ownership positions in companies there.

units.notes:
Teamwork has never been more important, in manufacturing (self-directed teams) and in the knowledge economy. A group is a collection of individuals; a team is a cohesive coalition working toward a shared agenda.

Tuckman's stages of team development

StageWhat happens
FormingPolite stage: introductions, enthusiasm, team looks to the leader for structure
StormingWin-lose stage: members compete for control, clash, take sides; frustration about goals and roles
NormingTeam works well together; ground rules and shared responsibility; respect
PerformingSelf-directed, confident, getting results; little direction needed
Adjourning (added 1977)The team disbands at the end of the project

The stages are not linear. Adding a new member or a confusing new task can send the team back to an earlier stage (it may re-storm and re-form).

Katzenbach & Smith's team performance curve: from working group to high-performing team.

Team diversity

Diverse teams are better at decision making and problem solving: they focus more on facts, re-examine them, and avoid groupthink. They are also more innovative. McKinsey: top quartile for ethnic diversity in management 35% more likely to beat industry returns; gender diversity 15%.
units.trap:
Exam trap
A team that was performing gets new members and uncertainty appears about roles = it slides back to storming; agreeing shared working rules = norming (mock Q29).
terms: A cohesive coalition of people working together toward a shared agenda.
Polite first stage; team relies on the leader.
Members compete for control and clash.
Ground rules, shared responsibility and respect develop.
The team disbands at the end of a project.

units.notes:
Social network: a patterned set of relationships between two or more people (actors), drawn as a sociogram. Networks are “the invisible organization”: how communication and resources really flow.

Three advantages for leaders: access to information and knowledge · access to diverse skill sets · power.

Lexicon

TermMeaning
Actors / nodesThe people or groups in the network
TiesConnections. Direct (one link) or indirect (through others)
Strong tiesKnow each other well; frequent exchanges
Weak tiesKnow each other at least by reputation; no regular exchange. Granovetter: people find jobs mostly through weak ties.
Bridging tieGives non-redundant information and resources
Centrality / densityHow central an actor is / how many in the network are connected

Three principles (Kilduff & Tsai)

PrincipleMeaning
ReciprocityTrading favours of roughly equal value
ExchangeTrading favours with people who are different from you: more value from complementary resources
SimilarityTies form spontaneously between people with common backgrounds, values, interests (risk: echo chamber)

Ibarra's three types of networks

NetworkPurpose
OperationalGet your current work done efficiently (people who can block or support a project)
PersonalPersonal and professional development: referrals, outside information, coaching, mentoring (alumni groups, clubs, associations)
StrategicFigure out future priorities and challenges and get stakeholder support for them

Example from the slides: Barack Obama's 2008 campaign used social networking principles.
units.trap:
Exam traps
Contacts outside your firm for coaching and career advice = personal. Contacts that help you see future trends and opportunities = strategic (mock Q30). Colleagues you need for today's tasks = operational.
terms: A patterned set of relationships between two or more actors.
Actors who know each other well and exchange often.
Actors who know each other but don't exchange regularly.
A tie providing non-redundant information and resources.
Trading favours of relatively equal value.
Trading favours with people different from you, for complementary resources.
Ties develop between people with common backgrounds and interests.
Contacts that help you get your current work done.
Contacts for development, referrals, coaching and mentoring.
Contacts that help you see future priorities and gain support.

units.notes:
Innovative culture: a work environment that fosters and rewards employee creativity instead of focusing on deadlines and revenue. Five traits: unique strategy, autonomy, trust, accepting failures, leadership.

Benefits (Swisher): sets a course for improvement · develops new ideas · company growth · competitive advantage · team efficiency · adaptive nature · attracts talent · improves the brand.

How leaders nurture innovation

MethodExample
Internal collaborationCross-departmental teams; R&D spends ~10% of its time in marketing and sales
Innovation labs & intrapreneurshipEmployee ideas become spin-offs (LEGO's Future Lab)
Innovation timeGoogle and 3M: 15–20% of the week for side projects (Gmail)
Partnerships & acquisitionsShare the risk, or buy small innovative firms (Cisco)
Open labs for co-creationCustomers co-create (BMW, Co-Create IKEA, LEGO Ideas)

Innovation portfolio: invest 70% core, 20% adjacent, 10% transformational; long-term returns are the reverse (10 / 20 / 70).

Seven reasons for failure to innovate

Fear of taking risks · lack of market orientation (no real customer value) · failure to scale · poor organizational structure and processes · wrong decisions · lack of internal communication · low priority for innovation. Usually failure comes from implementation, not the idea.
units.trap:
Exam trap
A product nobody needs because it isn't different from what exists = lack of market orientation, not fear of risk.
terms: Work environment that fosters and rewards creativity rather than focusing on deadlines and revenue.
An employee's idea becomes a spin-off or subsidiary led by that employee.
Free time for employees to work on innovative side projects.
Developing ideas together with customers, suppliers or partners.
Not understanding customer needs, so the product offers no real value.

units.notes:
The innovation network (McKinsey)

Connections and networks matter more for innovation than individual creativity. Four steps:

StepWhat
1. ConnectIdentify people with an innovation mind-set from different backgrounds
2. Set boundaries and engageDefine goals and how they link to strategy, mission and vision; time frames
3. Support and governLeadership structure, protocols, resources, sponsorship from top leaders
4. Manage and trackRewards for members, tracking progress, joining and leaving

Archetypes in the network: idea generators, researchers, experts, producers.

Organizational change

Organizational change: the movement of an organization from one state of affairs to another. Often required by a change in the environment. It can affect structure, strategy, policies, technology or culture; radical or incremental.

DriverExample
Workplace demographicsAgeing workforce, too few young workers
TechnologyMoore's law; music industry vs Napster
GlobalizationOutsourcing and offshoring
Market conditionsAirlines after 9/11 and fuel price rises
GrowthWidmer Brothers: garage to 11th largest US brewery
Poor performancePoor performers change more easily; success breeds overconfidence and inertia: “nothing fails like success” (Polaroid). New CEOs also trigger change.
terms: Network of innovators built in four steps: connect, set boundaries and engage, support and govern, manage and track.
Movement of an organization from one state of affairs to another.
Successful firms resist change through overconfidence and inertia.

units.notes:
Four reactions to change

ReactionBehaviour
Active resistanceMost negative: sabotages, objects openly, encourages others to resist
Passive resistanceDisturbed but silent: dislikes it quietly, stressed, may look for another job without telling anyone
ComplianceGoes along with little enthusiasm
Enthusiastic supportDefends the new way and encourages others to support it (the exception)

Seven reasons people resist

ReasonExample
Disrupted habitsAutomatic routines broken (automatic → stick shift)
PersonalityLow openness, low self-esteem, risk avoidance
Feelings of uncertaintyA merger: nobody knows what happens to their job
Fear of failureExperts doubt they'll perform well in the new system
Personal impact of changePeople welcome changes that help them and resist ones that hurt them
Prevalence of changeToo many changes; fatigue and skepticism
Perceived loss of powerSupervisors lose authority when teams take over

Resistance is not always bad: it is valuable feedback, and the most loyal employees may be the loudest critics. Example: the faster Dvorak keyboard never replaced QWERTY because of resistance.
units.trap:
Exam trap
The difference between active and passive is voice: loud objecting or sabotage is active, silent unhappiness is passive.
terms: Sabotaging or openly objecting and encouraging others to resist.
Disliking the change quietly without voicing it.
Going along with the change with little enthusiasm.
Defending the change and encouraging others to support it.
Resistance because there have been too many changes.
Resistance because the change reduces your authority or status.

units.t: Lewin's three stages & Kotter's eight steps
units.notes:
Lewin's three-stage model (1940s–50s)

StageActions
1. UnfreezePrepare people: communicate a plan and a vision, develop a sense of urgency, build a coalition of opinion leaders, give emotional and instrumental support (training), let employees participate
2. Change (move)Execute: continue to support, create small wins, eliminate obstacles
3. RefreezeMake it permanent: publicize success, reward change adoption

Contrast: the learning organization sees change as continuous rather than one episode.

Kotter's eight steps (1990s), mapped on Lewin

LewinKotter stepCase clue
Unfreeze1. Create urgencyShowing data, complaints, crisis, competitors, consequences of doing nothing
2. Build a guiding coalitionA small, influential group that leads the change
3. Form a strategic vision & initiativesA short statement of the desired future
4. Enlist a volunteer armyA large group of people who sign up to help
Change5. Enable action by removing barriersOld procedures or forms scrapped; staff empowered
6. Generate short-term winsA pilot with a visible, measurable result
7. Sustain accelerationUsing early success to roll out further
Refreeze8. Institute changeWritten into hiring, training, job descriptions, reviews

Memory hook: “Ugly Cats Vote Very Badly When Angry Indoors.”
units.trap:
Exam traps
Small leading group = guiding coalition; a big crowd of volunteers = volunteer army.
Presenting waiting times and complaints = create urgency (mock Q34). A measurable pilot result = short-term win (mock Q35).
terms: Preparing people so they are ready for and open to change.
Making the change permanent so new habits become the norm.
Kotter 2: a group with enough power and credibility to lead the change.
Kotter 4: a large base of people who act on the vision.
Kotter 6: visible early results that are rewarded.
Kotter 8: anchoring new behaviours in the culture.
Embraces continuous change instead of one-off episodes.

units.t: Schein's culture change & comparing the models
units.notes:
Schein's culture change process (six steps)

StepBook example
1. Create a sense of urgencyLou Gerstner used IBM's crisis to get buy-in
2. Change leaders and other key playersDisney's new CEO Iger removed the planning unit close to the old CEO
3. Role modelingIger joined game creation himself; bad example: HP executives' spying scandal
4. TrainingNASA safety training after Columbia; Midas customer training
5. Change the reward systemCommission → salary for customer focus; team bonuses for a team culture
6. Create new symbols and storiesContinental Airlines burned its 800-page manual (new one: 80 pages)

Memory hook: “Ugly Lions Rarely Take Rainy Showers.”

Comparing the three models

ModelWhenFocus
Lewin1940s–50s3 stages; general framework for any change; overcoming resistance
Schein1980s–906 steps; changing culture: values, role models, symbols
Kotter1990s8 steps; roadmap for large-scale transformation

bank.q: Management is best described as:

o: Set standards, compare actual performance, take corrective action

o: Revenue, costs and profit over three reporting years

bank.x: Interpersonal, informational, decisional. Technical/interpersonal/conceptual is Katz.

A line manager:
o: Leads a function that contributes directly to the organization's products or services

o: A clearly identifiable revenue-producing unit, such as a store or product line
Only the HR department and the hiring and training of all new employees
Coordinating one small team of specialists inside a single function or department
Writing the vision and mission of the whole organization with the board
bank.x: General manager = a revenue-producing unit, decisions across functions.

bank.q: According to Katz, which skill becomes MORE important the higher a manager rises?
o: None: all three stay equally important
bank.x: Higher up: more conceptual, fewer technical skills.

bank.q: In which Mintzberg role does a manager receive and collect information?
A manager studies customer complaints and industry reports to spot developments that may affect the organization. Which Mintzberg role?
The CEO cuts the ribbon at the opening of a new factory. Which Mintzberg role?
A manager decides how next year's budget is divided across three departments. Which role?
bank.x: Choosing where effort and money go = resource allocator.

bank.q: A supplier strike threatens production, and the manager quickly arranges an emergency alternative. Which role?
bank.x: Dealing with threats and crises = disturbance handler.

bank.q: After a board meeting, a manager shares the key decisions with her own team. Which role?
bank.x: Passing information INTO the organization = disseminator.

bank.q: A manager gives a press interview about the company's new sustainability results. Which role?
bank.x: Passing information OUT to the environment = spokesperson.

bank.q: A manager starts a project to launch a home-delivery service. Which role?
A workshop supervisor shows apprentices how to diagnose an engine fault with the scanner. Which Katz skill is she mainly using?
Which statement about Mintzberg's roles is correct?
o: The leader role is important at every level of management
Supervisors spend more time as figurehead than top managers do
The negotiator role belongs to the informational group
The disseminator sends the organization's information to the press
bank.x: Leadership runs through all levels. Supervisors do less figurehead work; negotiator is decisional; disseminator is internal.

bank.q: A CEO spends most of her week on long-term strategy and policies; a team leader spends his week fixing machines with his team. According to Katz:
o: The CEO relies most on conceptual skills, the team leader on technical skills
Both rely mainly on technical skills
The CEO relies most on technical skills, the team leader on conceptual skills
bank.x: Top = conceptual; lower level = technical; interpersonal matters for both.

bank.q: Which statement correctly separates two Mintzberg roles?
o: The disseminator passes information into the organization; the spokesperson passes it out to the environment
The disseminator passes information out to the press; the spokesperson passes it inward to the team
Both are decisional roles, because each of them decides which information is shared
Both are interpersonal roles, because each of them involves talking to other people inside and outside
bank.x: Both are informational: disseminator = inside, spokesperson = outside.

bank.q: A manager meets managers of other companies at an industry event to build contacts that can help her unit later. Which role and group?
bank.x: Interacting with people outside the unit = liaison, an interpersonal role.

bank.q: Personality is defined as:
o: A person's relatively stable feelings, thoughts and behavioural patterns
A person's current opinions about their job, colleagues and manager
The emotional attachment someone feels toward their employer and its goals
The skills and knowledge a person learned at school and at work
bank.x: Personality = relatively stable feelings, thoughts and behaviour.

bank.q: Which list contains exactly the Big Five personality traits?
Which Big Five trait predicts job performance across nearly all occupations?
bank.x: Conscientiousness is the one trait that uniformly predicts performance.

bank.q: For which Big Five trait is scoring high generally undesirable?
Self-efficacy is:
o: The belief that you can perform a specific task successfully
Overall positive feelings about yourself and your worth
The ability to adjust your behaviour to each social situation
The inclination to fix what is wrong without being asked to
bank.x: Self-efficacy is task-specific. The others are self-esteem, self-monitoring and proactive personality.

bank.q: Values are best defined as:
o: People's stable life goals, reflecting what is most important to them
Short-term moods and emotions that people experience at work during the day
The rules and procedures written in a company's employee handbook
The skills, knowledge and abilities required to do a job well

bank.q: Lena is curious, creative and loves learning new tools. Which Big Five trait does she score high on?
bank.x: Curious, creative, open to new ideas = openness.

bank.q: An employee consistently prepares carefully, meets deadlines and follows through on commitments. Which characteristic is predominant?
bank.x: Organized and dependable = conscientiousness. Commitment is an attitude toward the company.

bank.q: Tom is often anxious, irritable and moody at work. Which trait does he score high on?
A salesperson is outgoing, talkative and loves meeting new clients. Which trait?
bank.x: Outgoing and sociable = extraversion (good in sales).

bank.q: Without being asked, an employee notices a broken process and fixes it. Which personality dimension?
bank.x: Taking initiative to fix what is wrong = proactive personality.

bank.q: Sara is confident she can master Excel quickly but doubts she could give a good presentation. This illustrates:
Mark acts like a 'social chameleon', reading each situation and adjusting how he comes across. He is high in:
bank.x: High self-monitors adjust their behaviour to the situation.

bank.q: Which statement about personality testing in selection is correct?
o: Personality explains only about 10–15% of job performance; cognitive ability predicts better
Personality tests cannot be faked, which makes them more reliable than interviews
Personality is the strongest single predictor of job performance in every occupation studied
Personality tests are never controversial, so firms can use them without any concern
bank.x: Book: modest correlations, faking is possible, cognitive ability predicts better.

bank.q: A team avoids challenging the status quo because members dislike conflict. Which trait, despite its benefits, is linked to this drawback?
bank.x: Agreeable people are less likely to engage in constructive, change-oriented communication.

bank.q: Which statement about personality is correct?
o: It is relatively stable but can change over long periods
It is fixed after childhood and never changes afterwards
It is the same thing as a person's values
It always determines behaviour regardless of the job
bank.x: Stable but changes slowly; job demands also shape behaviour.

bank.q: What is organizational commitment?
o: The emotional attachment people have to the company they work for
The pay level and benefits an employee receives from the company
Compliance with organizational rules, policies and procedures
The list of tasks and responsibilities in a job description
bank.x: Emotional attachment: believes in the values, puts in effort, wants to stay.

bank.q: Job satisfaction refers to:
o: The feelings people have toward their job
How long someone stays with a company
The match between skills and job demands
bank.x: Job satisfaction = feelings toward the job.

bank.q: An attitude is:
o: Our opinions, beliefs and feelings about aspects of our environment
A stable personality trait that people are largely born with
A formal description of the tasks and duties of a job
A company's written policy about how employees should behave toward each other

bank.q: The psychological contract is:
o: The unspoken understanding of what employee and organization will give each other
The signed employment contract that lists salary, working hours, holidays and the notice period
A personality test used in hiring to predict whether a candidate will stay
The company's written code of conduct that every employee must sign
bank.x: Unspoken expectations: effort and loyalty for pay, raises, security.

bank.q: Person-organization fit is:
o: The match between a person's values, personality and goals and those of the organization
The match between a person's skills and abilities and the demands of the job
The number of years someone has worked for the same company and their loyalty to it over time
A person's fit with the personality and working style of their direct manager
bank.x: P-O fit = values with the organization. Skills with the job = P-J fit.

bank.q: Which job characteristic is linked to higher satisfaction and commitment?
bank.x: The job characteristics are skill variety, autonomy, feedback and significance. Justice and stress are separate factors.

bank.q: Employees learn that promotions were decided by drawing names from a hat. Which type of justice is violated?
bank.x: An unfair decision-making process = procedural justice.

bank.q: A manager gives an employee a raise but tells her, 'Even you deserve something sometimes.' Which justice suffers?
bank.x: Lack of respect and dignity = interactional justice.

bank.q: Workers doing the same job feel their pay is unfair compared with colleagues. Which type of justice?
bank.x: Fairness of outcomes such as pay = distributive.

bank.q: Yara isn't sure what her responsibilities are since the reorganization. This stressor is:
Tim's manager wants him to work late, but his role as a parent requires him home by six. This is:
bank.x: Contradictory demands between roles = role conflict.

bank.q: HR meets every employee who resigns to learn why they're leaving. This tool is:
bank.x: Exit interviews are with departing employees.

bank.q: A creative risk-taker joins a nuclear power plant where routine and predictability are key. The most likely problem is:
bank.x: His traits don't match the organization's values.

bank.q: Which statement about the attitude-behaviour link is correct?
o: Attitudes predict intentions better than actual behaviour, because the situation also matters
Dissatisfied employees always quit, so attitudes predict turnover perfectly
Attitudes have no relation to behaviour, so measuring them in employee surveys is mostly pointless
Attitude surveys work best when answers are shared with the direct manager
bank.x: A dissatisfied employee intends to leave; leaving depends on alternatives. Surveys work best when confidential.

bank.q: According to the interactionist perspective:
o: Behaviour is a function of the person and the situation interacting
Behaviour depends only on personality, whatever the situation is
Behaviour depends only on the job and the rules of the organization
Fit between person and organization doesn't affect attitudes
bank.x: Person × situation; fit increases satisfaction and commitment.

bank.q: An employee says 'we have great benefits here' and stays despite a better offer elsewhere. This mainly shows:
bank.x: Using 'we' and wanting to stay are signs of commitment.

bank.q: Leadership is defined in the course as:
o: The act of influencing others to work toward a goal
Holding the highest formal position in an organization
Controlling the budget and deciding how it is spent
Following the rules and making sure others do too

bank.q: Which five sources of power did French and Raven identify?
bank.x: French & Raven: reward, coercive, referent, expert, legitimate.

bank.q: An informal leader:
o: Has no formal position of authority but influences others through personal power
Is appointed by top management to lead the group alongside the formal leader
Only uses coercive power, because no rewards or formal authority are available to them
Is the official leader of the group as recognized by people outside it
bank.x: Informal leaders are acknowledged by the group, not appointed.

bank.q: Coercive power is:
o: The ability to punish or take away something people value
The ability to give rewards such as pay rises and promotions
Power that comes from a person's specialized expertise
Power that comes from being liked, admired and identified with

bank.q: A sales manager can assign desirable territories and performance bonuses to employees who achieve agreed targets. Which source of power?
bank.x: Giving rewards others want = reward power.

bank.q: A cybersecurity specialist influences the executive team because of her knowledge, although she holds no managerial position. Which power?
Colleagues follow Ahmed's lead because they admire him and want to be like him. Which power?
Employees follow the new director's instructions mainly because she is 'the boss' by title. Which power?
bank.x: The right to influence from a formal position = legitimate.

bank.q: A team member without any title becomes the person everyone turns to during a crisis project. She is best described as:
bank.x: She arises from the group's dynamics and has no formal position.

bank.q: A manager assumes employees dislike work and need tight control, so he checks everything. This reflects:
Which statement about the effects of power is correct?
o: Coercive power tends to alienate followers; referent and expert power lead to better results
Coercive power is the most effective way to build long-term commitment among followers in most firms
Legitimate power alone is enough for a leader to succeed in almost any situation
Reward power always creates deep, lasting commitment to the leader's goals
bank.x: Book: coercion alienates; referent and expert power work best; legitimate alone is rarely enough.

bank.q: A project manager can't give bonuses or punish anyone, but the team follows her because she knows the software best and they like her. Which combination?
Which statement best describes the leadership process (Hollander & Julian)?
o: A dynamic exchange relationship built over time between leader and followers
A one-way order from the leader to the followers, who carry it out
A fixed set of traits that a leader is born with and cannot develop
A formal title the organization gives someone, together with the authority that comes with it
bank.x: Leadership is a two-way, dynamic relationship built over time.

bank.q: Theory Y leaders typically:
o: Give employees discretion and involve them, believing people are self-directed and creative
Closely supervise employees, believing people dislike work and avoid responsibility
Rely mainly on coercive power and punishment to keep people productive and on schedule
Avoid any participation of employees, because decisions belong to managers

bank.q: The trait approach to leadership asks:
o: Which personal characteristics make someone a (successful) leader?
What do effective leaders actually do differently from other people?
Which situation calls for which leadership style to be effective?
How do followers judge the fairness of their leader's decisions?
bank.x: Traits: who is a leader. Behavioural: what leaders do.

bank.q: Task-oriented leader behaviours involve:
o: Structuring roles, giving instructions and pushing group performance
Showing concern for employees' feelings and treating them with respect
Leaving decisions entirely to the team with minimal involvement
Serving employees' personal needs and development before results

bank.q: People-oriented leader behaviours involve:
o: Showing concern for employee feelings and treating them with respect
Setting deadlines, assigning tasks and structuring subordinates' roles
Deciding alone and announcing the decision to the team afterwards
Punishing poor performance to keep standards high in the group

bank.q: Laissez-faire decision-making means:
o: Employees decide with minimal guidance from the leader
The leader decides alone and informs the employees
Employees participate, but the leader takes the final decision
The leader and team vote, and the majority decides

bank.q: Which Big Five trait has the strongest relationship with leader emergence and effectiveness?
A manager sets clear weekly targets, assigns each person's tasks and checks progress every Friday. Which behaviour?
bank.x: Structuring roles and checking performance = task-oriented.

bank.q: A supervisor regularly asks how her staff are doing, listens to personal worries and treats everyone with respect. Which behaviour?
The head chef decides the new menu alone and announces it to the kitchen. Which decision-making style?
bank.x: Deciding alone without involving employees = authoritarian.

bank.q: A team leader holds a vote with the team on which supplier to choose and follows the outcome. Which style?
bank.x: Employees participate in the decision = democratic.

bank.q: A manager tells the team 'decide among yourselves how to run the project' and gives no further input. Which style?
Which statement about the behavioural approach is correct?
o: People-oriented behaviour raises satisfaction, task-oriented slightly raises productivity, neither always works
Task-oriented behaviour always leads to the highest satisfaction and the highest productivity
Showing both behaviours at the same time guarantees effective leadership in every situation and team
Laissez-faire has the best track record of the three decision-making styles in research
bank.x: Both help for different purposes; the approach ignored context; laissez-faire has the worst record.

bank.q: According to Kirkpatrick and Locke, which set lists core leadership traits?
o: Drive, motivation to lead, integrity, self-confidence, cognitive ability, business knowledge
Height, age, wealth, gender, physical appearance and family background
Agreeableness, modesty, conflict avoidance, patience and a calm voice
Charm, luck, extraversion, humour, ambition, a strong network and an impressive physical presence
bank.x: Locke's core traits give leadership potential.

bank.q: What was the main limitation of both the trait and the behavioural approaches?
o: They ignored the situation (context) in which leaders operate
They focused too much on followers and too little on leaders
They were based almost only on studies of women leaders
They only studied military leaders in times of war
bank.x: Neither specified the conditions under which traits or behaviours work.

bank.q: Goleman argues about intelligence and leadership that:
o: IQ is a threshold for management, but emotional intelligence separates effective leaders
IQ is the only trait that really matters, because leaders must constantly solve complex business problems
Emotional intelligence is irrelevant for leaders, because it cannot be measured
High IQ guarantees leadership success once someone reaches top management
bank.x: IQ is a threshold; EQ differentiates.

bank.q: Transformational leaders:
o: Align employees' goals with the company's, so they focus on the company's well-being
Give rewards in exchange for the right behaviour and correct mistakes when needed, using clear agreements
Wait until something goes wrong before they step in and take action
Leave employees to decide everything with minimal guidance or involvement

bank.q: Which are the four tools of transformational leaders?
o: Charisma, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, individualized consideration
Contingent rewards, active and passive management by exception, punishment
Planning, organizing, leading and controlling the work of followers and their teams
Reward, coercive, expert and referent power used in the right order

bank.q: The key advice of authentic leadership is:
bank.x: Authentic = self-aware and true to your values.

bank.q: Servant leadership defines the leader's role as:
o: Serving others and helping employees develop and reach their goals
Controlling performance closely and correcting deviations early, before they grow
Inspiring followers with a magnetic, charismatic personality
Exchanging rewards for results that meet the agreed targets

bank.q: Passive management by exception means the leader:
o: Waits until something goes wrong before stepping in
Predicts problems early and prevents them from happening
Shows personal concern for each follower
bank.x: Passive MBE is the only transactional method that isn't effective.

bank.q: A leader asks employees to challenge established assumptions and develop original solutions instead of following procedures. Which kind of leadership?
bank.x: Intellectual stimulation is a transformational tool.

bank.q: A sales director pays a bonus to every rep who exceeds the quarterly target. Which approach?
bank.x: Rewards for accomplishments = contingent rewards, transactional.

bank.q: A manager leaves her team to work but keeps scanning for risks and steps in before small issues become problems. This is:
A CEO who grew up watching his father struggle without health insurance gives every part-time worker full benefits, true to that experience. Which approach?
bank.x: Howard Schultz: leading from your own life experience and values.

bank.q: A hospital manager spends hours coaching each nurse on their career goals and sometimes sacrifices her own time to help them succeed. Which approach?
A manager has a close, trust-based relationship with three team members who go beyond their job descriptions, and a purely formal one with the others. Which theory explains this?
bank.x: High- and low-quality LMX relationships (in-group vs out-group).

bank.q: Why is transformational leadership often more effective than transactional leadership?
o: Followers trust them more, because they show care and appeal to values
Transformational leaders use more punishment, so followers work harder
Transactional leadership never works, so any alternative is better
Transformational leaders don't set goals, so followers feel less pressure
bank.x: Trust is the key factor; transactional (except passive MBE) also works.

bank.q: Which statement about charisma is correct?
o: Charisma can be trained, isn't required for effectiveness and has a dark side
Charisma is purely genetic, so it cannot be developed through training
Charismatic CEOs always improve their company's future performance and share price
Charisma is the same as transactional leadership with a strong personality
bank.x: Book: trainable, not necessary, and harmful leaders can be charismatic too.

bank.q: A leader combines a bonus system for targets with an inspiring vision and personal coaching. The book's advice on this mix is:
o: Good: leaders should show both transformational and transactional behaviour
Bad: the two styles cancel each other out, so the leader should choose one
Only acceptable in the public sector, where bonuses are tied to clear rules
Bad: transactional behaviour always harms the trust built by the vision

bank.q: Which three values-based leadership styles did Copeland find most effective?
Ethical leadership is defined as:
o: Showing appropriate conduct and promoting it to followers through two-way communication
Maximizing shareholder value while staying within the limits of the law
Being yourself and true to your values, regardless of the context and the people you work with
Rewarding people for hitting their targets and correcting them when they fail

bank.q: Which trends are among the book's top five CHALLENGE trends?
o: Increasing concern for the environment and increasing competition for talent
Becoming more connected and becoming more mobile in how and where we work
Rise of the creative class and increasing collaboration inside organizations
Becoming more global and more connected through technology and trade
bank.x: Challenges: environment, personalization, pace of innovation, complexity, competition for talent.

bank.q: Which is one of Dillon and Bourke's six characteristics of inclusive leaders?
bank.x: The six Cs: commitment, courage, cognizance of bias, curiosity, cultural intelligence, collaborative.

bank.q: In the SCQA framework for ethical decisions, SCQA stands for:
Ethnocentrism is:
o: The belief that your own culture's norms are superior to all others
Respect for all cultures and openness to learning from them
A type of matrix structure used by multinational companies
A GLOBE dimension measuring how future-oriented and planning-focused a society is

bank.q: A multinational can legally use a low-cost production process in one country, but it seriously harms local communities. What makes this an ethical dilemma?
o: The decision involves competing economic and stakeholder responsibilities
The local culture automatically determines what the right decision is
The company lacks the authority to choose its own production method
It can be solved simply by choosing the cheapest legal option available

bank.q: A CEO openly admits in a town hall that she doesn't have all the answers and shares her own mistakes. This shows:
bank.x: Taking emotional risks by sharing weaknesses = vulnerability.

bank.q: An inclusive leader introduces anonymous CV screening because she knows personal and organizational biases affect hiring. Which C is this?
bank.x: Awareness of bias + structures to prevent it.

bank.q: A leader learns about her team members' cultural norms and adjusts her style to them. Which inclusive-leadership characteristic?
bank.x: Understanding other cultures and adapting = cultural intelligence.

bank.q: Before deciding whether to close a factory, a manager first lists all stakeholders and considers the situation from each one's point of view. Which part of the ethical decision process is this?
o: Monitoring the outcomes of the decision (answer)
bank.x: Step two: identify stakeholders and see it from their view.

bank.q: A company leads a movement for plastic-free oceans. Its leaders rely mostly on charisma instead of formal authority. This illustrates:
o: A corporation as a social movement
bank.x: Social movements depend on charisma rather than authority.

bank.q: Which pair correctly classifies two of the book's global trends?
o: Faster pace of innovation: challenge · Rise of the creative class: solution
Increasing collaboration: challenge · Increasing complexity: solution
Becoming more mobile: challenge · Greater personalization: solution
Increasing competition for talent: solution · Becoming more global: challenge
bank.x: Check both halves: innovation pace is a challenge, the creative class a solution.

bank.q: Which description fits transformational leadership in Copeland's values-based view (Bass & Riggio)?
o: Motivating others through a common mission that empowers them to develop as leaders
Being aware of one's own thoughts and behaviour and of the context one works in
Demonstrating appropriate conduct and promoting it to followers through two-way communication
Rewarding employees for meeting targets and correcting them when they miss them
bank.x: The others are authentic, ethical and transactional.

bank.q: Which are the components of the communication process?
o: Sender, message, channel, receiver, noise (and feedback)
Strategy, structure, systems, staff, skills (and style)
bank.x: Sender encodes → message → channel → receiver decodes; noise distorts.

bank.q: Which are the three main functions of communication in an organization?
o: Transmitting information, coordinating effort, sharing emotions
Hiring, training and promoting the right employees
Planning, budgeting and reporting results to shareholders and the board
Selling, buying and negotiating with partners

bank.q: Noise in the communication process is:
o: Anything that interferes with or distorts the message
Only the loud sounds in an open-plan office
The feedback the receiver sends back to the sender after decoding the message
The channel used to deliver the message
bank.x: Noise can be in the environment, the receiver or the sender.

bank.q: Information overload is:
o: Receiving more information than you can take in
Using words that mean different things to different people

bank.q: About what share of in-person communication comes from nonverbal cues, according to the slides?
bank.x: 55% nonverbal; only 7% from the words themselves.

bank.q: Before presenting a proposal, a manager turns his ideas into words, diagrams and tables. Which part of the communication process is this?
bank.x: The sender translates ideas into symbols = encoding.

bank.q: Two employees hear the same announcement. One sees an opportunity, the other a threat because of previous experiences. Which barrier explains the difference?
bank.x: Interpreting to fit your own beliefs and experiences = selective perception.

bank.q: Which of these is a nonverbal communication cue?
bank.x: Text and memo are written; a phone call is verbal.

bank.q: A department head tells her boss only the good news about a project so he won't get upset. Which barrier?
bank.x: Distorting or withholding to manage a reaction = filtering.

bank.q: A furious customer service agent ignores most of what her manager says during feedback. Which barrier?
bank.x: An upset receiver distorts or ignores the message.

bank.q: A manager must tell an employee he didn't get the promotion. Which channel is most appropriate?
o: A group e-mail to the team
bank.x: Emotional messages need rich, verbal channels.

bank.q: A customer service representative sends a suggestion directly to the head of the manufacturing department. Which direction of communication?
Which channel has the LOWEST information richness?
o: A video call with the team
A phone call with the manager
bank.x: Formal documents and spreadsheets are the leanest.

bank.q: A young employee uses slang that his older colleagues interpret differently. Which pair describes the barrier and the stage where it hits?
o: Differences in meaning (semantics), at the receiver's decoding
Filtering of information, at the sender's encoding stage
Information overload, in the channel the message travels through
Selective perception, in the feedback the receiver sends back
bank.x: Different meanings for words → wrong decoding by the receiver.

bank.q: According to the book, when should you choose written over verbal communication?
o: When you mainly want to convey facts; verbal is better for feelings
When the message is emotional and you want to show empathy and personal care
When you want the receiver to get maximum nonverbal information
Never: verbal communication is always better than written

bank.q: Decision making refers to:
o: Making choices among alternatives, which may include inaction
Following a manager's order without questioning it or looking at other options
Collecting information without choosing between options
Only the long-term strategic planning of top managers

bank.q: Programmed decisions are:
o: Decisions that occur often enough that we develop an automated response
Unique, important decisions that need careful analysis every single time they occur
Decisions made only by computers without any human involvement
Long-term strategic decisions taken by the top management team

bank.q: To satisfice means to:
o: Accept the first alternative that meets your minimum criteria
Search all alternatives to find the best possible one
Decide by gut feeling, based on experience and recognizing familiar patterns
Let the group vote and follow the majority decision

bank.q: Groupthink is:
o: The tendency to avoid critically evaluating ideas the group favours
Some members putting in less effort because others will do the work
Generating as many ideas as possible without judging them
Deciding by majority vote after a short group discussion

bank.q: In the creative decision-making model, which step follows immersion?
bank.x: Problem identification → immersion → incubation → illumination → verification.

bank.q: Decisions that employees make every day to run the organization are:
bank.x: Strategic sets the course, tactical = how, operational = daily.

bank.q: A restaurant automatically reorders a standard quantity of ingredients whenever inventory reaches a set level. What type of decision is this?
bank.x: Recurring with an automated rule = programmed.

bank.q: During a management meeting, members with doubts stay silent because they want to keep agreement with the majority. Which problem?
A company keeps investing in a failing IT project because it has already spent €2 million on it. This is:
bank.x: Continuing a failing course because of past investment.

bank.q: An experienced ER doctor decides in seconds which patient to treat first, based on pattern recognition. Which model?
bank.x: Gut feeling and experience under time pressure = intuitive.

bank.q: A team first writes ideas down individually and silently, then shares them, discusses them and votes. Which technique?
bank.x: NGT: write alone → share → discuss → vote.

bank.q: Experts in different countries answer a series of written questionnaires until they reach consensus, without ever meeting. Which technique?
A buyer judges every supplier's offer against the first price she heard, even though it was unusually high. Which bias?
bank.x: Relying too heavily on one piece of information.

bank.q: When should you use the rational decision-making model?
o: When information can be quantified, the decision is important and you want the best outcome
When there is extreme time pressure, goals are unclear and you must act on experience
When minimum criteria are clear and you have little time to compare every option
When no solution exists yet and the group first needs many new, creative ideas to choose from
bank.x: Others describe intuitive, bounded rationality and creative.

bank.q: Which pair correctly matches a group problem with its description?
o: Social loafing: some put in less effort · Groupthink: avoiding critical evaluation of favoured ideas
Social loafing: avoiding critical evaluation of favoured ideas · Groupthink: some put in less effort
Social loafing: generating too many ideas · Groupthink: generating too few ideas
Social loafing: a group decision rule · Groupthink: a creative decision technique

bank.q: Which is a real advantage of group decision making over individual decision making?
o: Implementation is easier because members are invested in the decision
Groups are always faster than individuals, because work is divided
Groups always outperform their best member on every type of task
Groups never suffer from process losses when all of their members are experienced experts
bank.x: Groups are slower, rarely beat their best member and do suffer process losses.

bank.q: A manager reasons after a failed launch: 'It was obvious this would fail.' Which bias?
A mission statement communicates:
o: The organization's reason for being and how it serves its stakeholders
What the organization wants to become in the future and its aspirations
The organization's core beliefs and principles that guide behaviour
The budget and financial targets for the next three years
bank.x: Mission = why we exist now. The future one is vision; beliefs are values.

bank.q: A vision statement is:
o: A future-oriented declaration of the organization's purpose and aspirations
A list of the company's products and services and the markets in which it sells them
The organization's reason for being and how its stakeholders are served
An analysis of the organization's internal strengths and weaknesses
bank.x: Vision = what we want to become.

bank.q: Stakeholders are best defined as:
o: Individuals or groups with an interest in the organization's ability to deliver results
Only the shareholders who own the company and receive its dividends
The top management team that formulates the strategy and makes sure it is implemented
Competitors in the same industry that fight for the same customers
bank.x: Customers, employees, investors, suppliers, government, communities.

bank.q: What is the correct order of the strategic management process?
o: Objectives & analysis → formulation → implementation → evaluation & control
