cases.title: PedalPoint
text: PedalPoint runs shared e-bikes in Rotterdam and Utrecht. Its mission is to make short city trips clean and affordable for residents. Riders unlock bikes with an app built by PedalPoint's in-house software team. Riders like the app, but almost every bike- and scooter-sharing competitor offers a very similar one.

Every night a crew collects empty batteries, charges them at a central depot and swaps them back before the morning rush, so bikes are always ready to ride. A separate purchasing team buys batteries and spare parts from approved suppliers.
Two other e-bike-sharing companies have announced they will launch in both cities next year. At the same time, the Dutch government is discussing a tax subsidy for people who commute by e-bike.

Management originally planned to target tourists in the city centres. Ride data, however, showed that most trips were commuters riding to train stations. Local managers moved bikes to stations and launched a monthly commuter pass, which now brings in most of the revenue.

qs.q: How is the nightly collection, charging and swapping of batteries best classified in the value chain?
o: Primary activity: operations, because it keeps the service working for customers
Support activity: procurement, because the batteries are bought from suppliers
Support activity: firm infrastructure, because it involves planning and scheduling
Support activity: human resource management, because a crew does the work
Primary activity: marketing & sales, because charged bikes attract more riders
Support activity: technology development, because batteries are a technology
qs.x: It directly creates and delivers the service the customer uses. Buying the batteries would be procurement, a different team in the case.

qs.q: Using VRIO, what does PedalPoint's unlock app give the company?
o: Competitive parity; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Sustained competitive advantage; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Temporary competitive advantage; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Unused competitive advantage; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Competitive disadvantage; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Synergy between its two cities; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
qs.x: Valuable (riders like it) but NOT rare (almost every competitor has one) → stop at R → parity.

qs.q: Which combination correctly classifies the two external developments?
o: New e-bike companies: threat of new entrants (Porter) · Commuting subsidy: political/economic opportunity (PESTEL)
New e-bike companies: bargaining power of buyers (Porter) · Commuting subsidy: political/economic opportunity (PESTEL)
New e-bike companies: threat of new entrants (Porter) · Commuting subsidy: internal strength (VRIO)
New e-bike companies: internal weakness (value chain) · Commuting subsidy: threat (Porter)
New e-bike companies: threat of substitutes (Porter) · Commuting subsidy: threat (PESTEL)
New e-bike companies: opportunity (PESTEL) · Commuting subsidy: bargaining power of suppliers (Porter)
qs.x: Both halves must be right: new firms launching = new entrants; a subsidy is external and helps = opportunity.

qs.q: How should the shift from tourists to the commuter pass be classified?
o: Emergent strategy that became part of the realized strategy; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Intended strategy, because management planned it from the start; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Deliberate strategy, because it followed the original plan; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Corporate strategy, because it decides which businesses to be in; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
A mission statement, because it explains why the company exists; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Functional strategy, because only the purchasing team was involved; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
qs.x: The tourist plan changed after experience and local managers adapted: emergent. What actually happened is the realized strategy.

cases.title: ClearSip
text: ClearSip sells refillable water bottles with a built-in filter that it designed and patented. No competitor has a comparable filter, and copying it would take years of research. ClearSip has a dedicated R&D team and a sales network that actively promotes the filter in every store.

Bottles are made in a factory in Eindhoven. A purchasing department negotiates with suppliers for plastics and filter materials. Customer support handles filter replacements and warranty claims after purchase.
Recently, the EU announced a ban on single-use plastic bottles from 2028. At the same time, a large supermarket chain, which sells 60% of ClearSip's bottles, demands a 15% price cut.
ClearSip's statement on its website reads: “By 2032, every household in Europe drinks clean water without a single plastic bottle.”

qs.q: Using VRIO, what does the patented filter give ClearSip?
o: Sustained competitive advantage; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Competitive parity; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Temporary competitive advantage; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Unused competitive advantage; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Competitive disadvantage; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Synergy; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
qs.x: Valuable, rare (no comparable filter), hard to imitate (years of research), organized (R&D team, active sales network).

qs.q: Handling filter replacements and warranty claims after purchase is which value-chain activity?
qs.x: After-sales support that keeps the product's value = service.

qs.q: Which combination correctly classifies the two external developments?
o: EU ban: legal opportunity (PESTEL) · Supermarket demand: bargaining power of buyers (Porter)
EU ban: legal opportunity (PESTEL) · Supermarket demand: bargaining power of suppliers (Porter)
EU ban: internal strength (VRIO) · Supermarket demand: bargaining power of buyers (Porter)
EU ban: threat of new entrants (Porter) · Supermarket demand: economic threat (PESTEL)
EU ban: legal threat (PESTEL) · Supermarket demand: rivalry among competitors (Porter)
EU ban: technological opportunity (PESTEL) · Supermarket demand: threat of substitutes (Porter)
qs.x: A ban on single-use bottles helps a refillable-bottle firm: legal opportunity. A big customer pushing prices down = buyer power.

qs.q: How should the statement on ClearSip's website be classified?
o: Vision statement, because it describes what the organization wants to achieve in the future; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Mission statement, because it describes why the company exists today and whom it serves; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Values statement, because it lists core beliefs; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Functional strategy, because it guides one department; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
A KPI, because it is measurable; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Stakeholder analysis, because it mentions households; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
qs.x: “By 2032…” is a future aspiration = vision.

cases.title: Noordwind Ferries
text: Noordwind Ferries operates passenger ferries between the Dutch mainland and three Wadden islands. The company's statement reads: “We connect island communities to the mainland with safe, reliable and affordable crossings, every day of the year.”

For years Noordwind has been the only operator, because the government grants ferry licences. Its tickets are the cheapest per kilometre in the region, made possible by standard ship designs, fully digital ticketing and very low overhead.

Noordwind also owns a small chain of island bike-rental shops. Ferry passengers who book a bike together with their ticket get a discount, and since the combined offer started, both the ferries and the bike shops sell more than before.

Next year the government will open the licences to competition, and two foreign operators are expected to bid. Meanwhile, interest rates have risen sharply, making the planned purchase of two new electric ferries much more expensive.

qs.q: How should Noordwind's statement be classified?
o: Mission statement, because it explains the company's reason for being and whom it serves; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Vision statement, because it describes a future the company wants to become; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Values statement, because it lists the core beliefs and principles the company stands for; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Corporate strategy, because it decides which businesses to be in; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
A SMART objective, because it has a deadline; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
A stakeholder analysis, because it names communities; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
qs.x: Present tense, purpose and who is served = mission.

qs.q: Which combination correctly classifies how Noordwind competes and what the bike-rental link shows?
o: Competes through cost leadership · The combined offer shows synergy
Competes through differentiation · The combined offer shows synergy
Competes through cost leadership · The combined offer shows a functional strategy
Competes through focus on luxury · The combined offer shows diversification only
Competes through differentiation · The combined offer shows competitive parity
Competes through cost leadership · The combined offer shows an emergent strategy
qs.x: Cheapest tickets from low costs = cost leadership. Both businesses selling more together than apart = synergy.

qs.q: Which combination correctly classifies the two developments in the last paragraph?
o: Licences opening up: threat of new entrants (Porter) · Higher interest rates: economic threat (PESTEL)
Licences opening up: threat of substitutes (Porter) · Higher interest rates: economic threat (PESTEL)
Licences opening up: bargaining power of buyers (Porter) · Higher interest rates: technological threat (PESTEL)
Licences opening up: internal weakness (SWOT) · Higher interest rates: economic opportunity (PESTEL)
Licences opening up: threat of new entrants (Porter) · Higher interest rates: internal weakness (value chain)
Licences opening up: rivalry among existing competitors (Porter) · Higher interest rates: legal threat (PESTEL)
qs.x: Foreign operators coming in = new entrants. Interest rates = economic, external, harmful.

cases.title: Brickly Toys
text: Brickly Toys produces wooden building sets. Its classic set has held a large share of the toddler-toy market for twenty years; that market barely grows, but the set earns most of Brickly's profit. Two years ago Brickly launched an app-connected robot kit in the fast-growing educational-tech market, where it still has only a small share.
Brickly's designers are known for their award-winning, child-safe designs. Several competitors have hired similar designers in the past year and now sell sets that parents find hard to tell apart.

The board's three-year plan was to sell mainly through toy stores. Store sales stayed flat, but teachers started ordering sets for classrooms. Brickly's regional sales managers responded with a school programme, which now generates a third of revenue.
Brickly is now discussing whether to keep, invest in or sell the robot kit.

qs.q: In the BCG matrix, how are the classic set and the robot kit best classified?
o: Classic set: cash cow · Robot kit: question mark
Classic set: star · Robot kit: dog
Classic set: dog · Robot kit: star
Classic set: cash cow · Robot kit: star
Classic set: question mark · Robot kit: cash cow
Classic set: star · Robot kit: question mark
qs.x: High share, low growth, profitable = cash cow. Low share, high growth = question mark.

qs.q: Using VRIO, what do Brickly's design skills give the company today?
o: Competitive parity, because competitors now have similar designers; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Sustained competitive advantage, because the designs keep winning awards; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Unused competitive advantage, because Brickly isn't organized; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Temporary competitive advantage that will last many years; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Competitive disadvantage, because the designs are not valuable; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Synergy, because design and sales work together; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
qs.x: Valuable, but no longer rare: competitors hired similar designers and sell look-alike sets → parity.

qs.q: How should the school programme be classified?
o: Emergent strategy that became part of the realized strategy; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Intended strategy, because the board planned it; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Deliberate strategy, because it was in the three-year plan; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Unrealized strategy, because store sales stayed flat; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
A vision statement, because it describes the future; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
Corporate strategy, because it is a new business; this classification explains how the case applies the concept
qs.x: Not in the board's plan; regional managers adapted to teacher demand = emergent, and it is now part of what actually happened.

cases.title: Rijnstad Hospital
text: Rijnstad Hospital still records patient information on paper. Nurses spend about 40 minutes per shift searching for files, and last year two medication errors were traced back to missing paperwork. A new national regulation requires all hospitals to use digital patient records by 2028.

The new director, Dr. Hendriks, opens the yearly staff meeting by showing the error reports, the time lost per shift, and a comparison with three hospitals that already went digital. She explains that the hospital could lose its accreditation if nothing changes.

She then asks a respected senior nurse, the head of IT, two doctors and a patient representative to lead the project together. This group writes a short statement: “Every patient's full story, safe and available in seconds.” They invite all departments to send volunteers, and more than 120 staff sign up as ‘digital champions’.

During the rollout, some doctors keep using paper and complain loudly in meetings, encouraging colleagues to do the same. Several older nurses say nothing but feel stressed, and two quietly apply for jobs elsewhere. Most administrative staff use the system as required, without much enthusiasm.

The hospital removes the old paper order forms and gives each ward two extra training days. After three months, the pilot ward reports that search time has fallen from 40 to 5 minutes, which is shared in the hospital newsletter. Finally, digital record-keeping is added to every job description and to the yearly performance review.

qs.q: Which Kotter step is represented by Dr. Hendriks presenting the error reports, lost time, other hospitals' results and the accreditation risk?
o: Create urgency; this classification identifies the step the case describes
Form a strategic vision and initiatives; this classification identifies the step the case describes
Build a guiding coalition; this classification identifies the step the case describes
Generate short-term wins; this classification identifies the step the case describes
Institute change; this classification identifies the step the case describes
Enable action by removing barriers; this classification identifies the step the case describes
qs.x: Showing the problem and the consequences of doing nothing = create urgency.

qs.q: Which part of the case most clearly represents Kotter's guiding coalition?
o: The senior nurse, head of IT, two doctors and patient representative who lead it
The 120 ‘digital champions’ who signed up from all departments to help colleagues
The statement “Every patient's full story, safe and available in seconds”
The pilot ward's drop in search time from 40 to 5 minutes, shared hospital-wide
The national regulation requiring all hospitals to use digital records by 2028
Adding digital record-keeping to job descriptions and annual performance reviews
qs.x: Small, influential group LEADING the change. The 120 champions are the volunteer army, the statement is the vision, the pilot a short-term win, job descriptions = institute change.

qs.q: Which combination correctly classifies the reactions of the doctors and of the older nurses?
o: Doctors: active resistance · Nurses: passive resistance
Doctors: passive resistance · Nurses: active resistance
Doctors: active resistance · Nurses: enthusiastic support
qs.x: Loud and recruiting others = active; silent, stressed, quietly leaving = passive.

qs.q: Adding digital record-keeping to every job description and review belongs to which Lewin stage and Kotter step?
o: Refreeze · Enable action by removing barriers
qs.x: Making the new behaviour permanent = refreeze and Kotter 8.

cases.title: Vesta Insurance
text: Vesta Insurance is known for slow, rule-heavy service. Customer complaints have doubled in two years while digital competitors win young customers. The board replaces the CEO with Sara Okafor, who previously led a fintech start-up.

In a town-hall meeting, Okafor tells all staff that at current trends Vesta will lose a third of its customers within three years. She replaces two senior directors who openly blocked earlier reforms. She personally spends one day a month answering customer calls and asks every manager to do the same.

All employees follow a customer-empathy training. Sales staff move from commission per policy sold to a fixed salary plus a bonus based on customer satisfaction. In front of all staff, Okafor shreds the 600-page claims manual and replaces it with a 40-page guide; the story spreads quickly through the company.
Some long-serving managers, who used to approve every claim personally, resist the new guide because front-line staff can now approve small claims themselves.

qs.q: Okafor personally answering customer calls every month best represents which step of Schein's culture change process?
o: Role modeling; this classification identifies the step the case describes
Training; this classification identifies the step the case describes
Changing the reward system; this classification identifies the step the case describes
Creating a sense of urgency; this classification identifies the step the case describes
Creating new symbols and stories; this classification identifies the step the case describes
Changing leaders and other key players; this classification identifies the step the case describes
qs.x: The leader shows the behaviour she expects.

qs.q: Shredding the 600-page manual in front of all staff best represents:
o: Changing leaders and other key players
qs.x: A dramatic, visible act that becomes a story. The question is about Schein, so stay in that model.

qs.q: Which combination correctly classifies (1) the town-hall warning and (2) replacing the two directors?
o: (1) Creating a sense of urgency · (2) Changing leaders and other key players
(1) Role modeling · (2) Changing leaders and other key players
(1) Creating a sense of urgency · (2) Changing the reward system
(1) Training in the new way of working · (2) Creating new symbols and stories
(1) Creating new symbols and stories · (2) Role modeling
(1) Changing the reward system · (2) Creating a sense of urgency
qs.x: Warning about losing customers = urgency; removing blockers = changing key players.

qs.q: Why do the long-serving managers most likely resist the new guide?
qs.x: They used to approve every claim; now front-line staff can. Their authority shrinks.

cases.title: GreenGrid Energy
text: GreenGrid is a Dutch energy supplier. Its customer service runs on a 20-year-old system, and in the last two years the company has reorganized its structure three times. When management announces a new customer platform, many employees sigh: “Here we go again.”

Management first explains why the change is needed: complaints have tripled and a new competitor offers instant online service. Team leaders who are respected by their colleagues are trained first so they can answer questions. Employees join workshops to help design the new screens, and everyone gets two days of hands-on training.

During the rollout, the project is split into four phases, and after each phase the time to solve a customer question is shown on screens in the office. A department that kept using the old workaround forms has them removed.
When the platform is fully running, management shares that customer satisfaction rose 18%, and the employees who helped colleagues most are thanked by name at the annual meeting.
Senior call agents, who know every trick of the old system, worry they will no longer be the experts people turn to.

qs.q: Employees sighing “Here we go again” after three reorganizations in two years best reflects which reason for resistance?
qs.x: Too many changes in a short time → fatigue and skepticism.

qs.q: Training respected team leaders first, workshops where employees help design the screens and two days of training all belong to which Lewin stage?
o: Unfreeze; this classification identifies the step the case describes
Change (move); this classification identifies the step the case describes
Refreeze; this classification identifies the step the case describes
Institute change (Kotter 8); this classification identifies the step the case describes
Sustain acceleration (Kotter 7); this classification identifies the step the case describes
Learning organization; this classification identifies the step the case describes
qs.x: Coalition of opinion leaders, participation and support before the change = unfreeze.

qs.q: Which combination correctly classifies (1) sharing the 18% satisfaction rise and (2) thanking helpful employees by name?
o: (1) Publicize success · (2) Reward change adoption, both refreezing
(1) Create small wins · (2) Eliminate obstacles, both changing
(1) Develop urgency · (2) Build a coalition, both unfreezing
(1) Publicize success · (2) Provide emotional support, both unfreezing
(1) Reward change adoption · (2) Publicize success, both changing
(1) Communicate a vision · (2) Allow participation, both refreezing
qs.x: After implementation: share results and reward adoption = refreeze.

qs.q: Why do the senior call agents most likely worry about the change?
o: Fear of failure, because they doubt their expertise will still count
Prevalence of change, because of the many earlier reorganizations
Personal impact, because they will get nicer offices after the move
Disrupted habits only, because they must drive to work differently
Enthusiastic support, because experienced agents like new tools
Compliance, because they go along with the change without enthusiasm
qs.x: Experts unsure whether their success will last under the new system = fear of failure.

cases.title: Polder Print
text: Polder Print is a large printing company that wants to become more innovative. Ideas from employees currently need approval from five management layers, and most ideas never get past the second layer. Each department competes for its own budget and rarely shares information with others.

The new innovation director first identifies twenty employees from different departments who are curious, comfortable with uncertainty and full of ideas. She then defines what the group should achieve and how its goals fit Polder Print's mission and five-year strategy, with clear deadlines.

Next, top management agrees to sponsor the group, gives it a budget, and sets rules for how ideas are shared and decided on. Finally, the group agrees how members will be recognized for their contributions and how progress will be tracked.
Polder Print also lets employees spend 10% of their week on their own projects and invites customers to an annual co-design day.

qs.q: The five approval layers and departments competing for their own budgets mainly illustrate which two reasons for failure to innovate?
o: Poor organizational structure and processes, and lack of internal communication
Fear of taking risks by managers, and failure to scale up successful pilots
Lack of market orientation among managers, and wrong decisions about which ideas to fund
Low priority for innovation in the strategy, and lack of market orientation
Failure to scale beyond the pilot phase, and poor structure and processes
Wrong decisions by the innovation board, and fear of taking risks
qs.x: Slow, layered processes = poor structure and processes; isolated, competing departments = lack of internal communication.

qs.q: Defining what the group should achieve and how its goals fit the mission and strategy, with deadlines, is which innovation network step?
o: Set boundaries and engage; this classification identifies the step the case describes
Connect; this classification identifies the step the case describes
Support and govern; this classification identifies the step the case describes
Manage and track; this classification identifies the step the case describes
Create urgency (Kotter); this classification identifies the step the case describes
Unfreeze (Lewin); this classification identifies the step the case describes
qs.x: Step 2: goals, link to strategy, mission and vision, time frames.

qs.q: Which combination correctly classifies the two practices in the last paragraph?
o: 10% own-project time: innovation time · Customer co-design day: open lab for co-creation
10% own-project time: internal collaboration · Customer co-design day: acquisition
10% own-project time: intrapreneurship spin-off · Customer co-design day: internal collaboration
10% own-project time: innovation time · Customer co-design day: failure to scale
10% own-project time: open lab · Customer co-design day: innovation time
10% own-project time: partnership · Customer co-design day: market orientation failure
qs.x: Free time for own projects = innovation time; customers helping design = co-creation.

rcase.title: SolarNest Energy
text: SolarNest Energy was founded eight years ago with the mission of making household energy independence affordable and understandable. The company installs residential solar panels, home batteries, and digital energy-management systems in three European countries. Its customers are mainly homeowners who want to reduce electricity costs and become less dependent on traditional utilities. SolarNest has grown quickly by combining equipment installation with ongoing technical support rather than simply selling individual products.

A central part of the service is SolarNest’s proprietary digital platform. The platform studies a household’s historical electricity use, weather forecasts, and changing energy prices. It then predicts future consumption and schedules battery charging or household energy use for lower-cost periods. The system has been improved using several years of customer data and is integrated with the company’s installation, maintenance, and customer-support processes. Competitors can buy similar panels and batteries, but they do not have access to SolarNest’s accumulated data, established algorithms, and integrated service routines.

SolarNest also has a certified installer network and strong working relationships with local municipalities. These relationships help the company navigate permits and safety requirements. Its reputation for dependable installation has created customer trust, although maintaining the network is expensive. The company’s website, marketing campaigns, and standard panel designs are professional but similar to those used by many competitors.

The external environment is becoming more challenging. A national government has announced that household solar subsidies will decline next year. Electricity prices remain volatile, and several large utility companies are entering the battery market. These utilities have strong brands and large customer bases. Customers are also asking more questions about data privacy, equipment origins, installation quality, and the environmental impact of battery production.

Senior leaders are reviewing SolarNest’s competitive position. Some favor rapid expansion into new countries. Others want to license the digital platform to utility companies, while a third group believes SolarNest should strengthen its existing markets. Before choosing a direction, management wants to distinguish ordinary resources from resources capable of supporting a sustained competitive advantage. The strategy team therefore examines whether each resource is valuable, rare, difficult to imitate, and supported by the organization.

The review must also separate temporary market benefits from internal strategic resources. Subsidies may increase demand, but competitors can receive them as well. Advertising can attract attention, but rival firms can imitate it quickly. Management therefore focuses on the combination of technology, accumulated information, organizational routines, and service integration that may be more difficult for competitors to reproduce.

Stakeholder expectations further complicate the choice. Municipal regulators have formal authority over permits and installation safety. Customers want affordable systems and clear privacy safeguards, employees want stable growth and training, and investors expect expansion without excessive risk. The strategy team maps each stakeholder according to power and interest. It also uses PESTEL to distinguish the political effect of changing subsidies from economic energy-price volatility, technological battery improvements, legal privacy requirements, social expectations, and environmental pressures. These classifications will help management interpret the case evidence consistently before selecting a strategic direction.

rcase.title: MedLink Connect
text: MedLink Connect provides a secure telehealth platform to hospitals, specialist clinics, and regional healthcare networks. Its mission is to improve access to medical expertise regardless of a patient’s location. The platform combines video consultations, appointment scheduling, secure messaging, and access to encrypted patient information. MedLink has built a reputation for reliable clinical support and has long-term partnerships with several teaching hospitals.

Demand for telehealth is growing in rural regions where patients often travel long distances to see specialists. Hospitals value MedLink’s understanding of clinical workflows and its ability to integrate with existing hospital systems. However, the competitive environment is changing. Global technology companies now offer basic video-consultation services at lower prices. Large hospital groups are negotiating more aggressively, and new European privacy requirements demand stronger controls over patient information.

The leadership team is considering expansion into two neighboring countries. This decision requires choices at several levels. The board and executive team must decide which countries MedLink should enter, how much capital to invest, and whether expansion should occur through partnerships or direct ownership. The telehealth business unit must determine how MedLink will compete against lower-cost platforms. It may emphasize clinical reliability, specialist integration, security, or price.

Individual departments must translate these broader choices into concrete actions. The marketing department will adapt communication for local healthcare systems. Human resources will identify the skills needed for international support. The cybersecurity department must implement stronger authentication, update incident-response procedures, train employees, and monitor compliance with the new privacy requirements. These actions must support the business unit’s competitive approach and the organization’s overall expansion priorities.

Some managers confuse these levels of strategy. They describe every important decision as “corporate strategy,” even when a decision concerns one department’s contribution. MedLink’s strategy director emphasizes that corporate strategy concerns the organization’s overall scope, business strategy concerns how a business competes, and functional strategy concerns how departments support the broader direction. The distinction is important because responsibilities, budgets, and performance measures must be assigned clearly before expansion begins.

During the planning meeting, the cybersecurity director presents a detailed departmental program covering encryption standards, access controls, employee training, supplier reviews, and incident reporting. The program does not decide which countries MedLink enters or the overall basis of competition. Instead, it explains how one specialist function will contribute to the broader strategic priorities established by senior and business-level management.

MedLink also reviews its external position. Because a small number of large hospital groups purchase most subscriptions, those buyers can negotiate strongly over price and service conditions. New privacy legislation raises mandatory compliance requirements, while advances in encryption, video quality, and system integration create technological opportunities. Managers therefore use Porter’s Five Forces to interpret bargaining pressure and PESTEL to separate legal change from technological development. The tools provide different but complementary explanations of the competitive environment facing the platform.

rcase.title: HarborTech Manufacturing
text: HarborTech Manufacturing produces navigation and communication equipment for commercial ships. Its products are known for reliability, but competitors have begun offering similar equipment at lower prices and with shorter delivery times. Several important customers have warned HarborTech that future contracts will depend on improved production speed and consistent quality. Internal reports also show that repetitive assembly work causes errors and employee injuries.

The leadership team proposes introducing collaborative robots on selected production lines. Unlike traditional industrial robots that operate separately from employees, collaborative robots can perform repetitive tasks alongside trained technicians. Management expects the technology to increase precision, reduce physical strain, and allow employees to focus on testing and complex technical work. However, the investment is expensive and requires major changes in skills, roles, and daily routines.

Employee reactions are mixed. Younger technicians are interested in learning robotics, while some experienced employees fear that automation will eventually eliminate their jobs. Union representatives ask for clear employment guarantees and meaningful involvement in implementation. Rumors spread that the company has already decided to reduce staffing, although senior leaders state that the current plan focuses on retraining rather than dismissal.

The chief operating officer begins the change process by presenting evidence. She shares data showing longer delivery times, rising error rates, physical strain, and lost customer contracts. She explains how competitors are using advanced production technology and why HarborTech cannot maintain its current methods without risking further decline. Managers organize workshops in which employees can discuss concerns and examine how future roles may change.

Only after these activities does HarborTech begin a supervised pilot on one production line. Employees receive training, safety procedures are tested, and the pilot team collects feedback. If the test succeeds, the new workflow will be expanded and eventually incorporated into job descriptions and performance systems. The leadership team uses Lewin’s model to distinguish preparation for change from implementation and later stabilization. It wants employees to understand why the first stage must weaken attachment to the existing situation before new behavior is introduced.

Leaders deliberately avoid presenting the robots as a completed decision requiring immediate compliance. They first challenge the belief that existing performance is acceptable and create awareness of the gap between current results and customer expectations. This preparation is intended to build readiness. Training, pilot testing, and formal reinforcement will follow, but they belong to later parts of the change process.

Resistance takes different forms. Some employees openly organize protests, representing active resistance. Others appear cooperative but quietly delay sharing information with the pilot team, representing passive resistance. Management wants the wider change to support innovation rather than fear. Leaders therefore propose safe experiments, cross-functional learning, transparent reporting, and recognition for responsible improvement ideas. Unsuccessful tests that follow agreed safety rules will be reviewed for learning instead of receiving automatic punishment. HarborTech sees this approach as a possible source of faster improvement, employee involvement, and competitive advantage.

rcase.title: FreshLoop Packaging
text: FreshLoop Packaging was created to reduce the amount of single-use packaging generated by supermarkets, restaurants, and takeaway services. The company supplies reusable food containers that customers can return after use. FreshLoop’s mission is to make reuse as convenient as disposal while maintaining strict standards for food safety. Its customers include several supermarket chains, workplace cafeterias, and more than two hundred independent restaurants

FreshLoop originally focused on container design and sales. The company developed a patented sealing system that keeps food fresh and reduces leakage. However, management soon discovered that a reusable container creates value only when customers can return it easily and the container can be prepared safely for another cycle. FreshLoop therefore built collection points near shops and restaurants. Returned containers are transported to regional cleaning hubs, where they are inspected, washed, sanitized, and prepared for recirculation.

The operational system is complex. Transport partners move containers between customers, collection points, and cleaning hubs. Employees at the hubs monitor hygiene, remove damaged products, and organize containers for delivery. The company’s technology team maintains tracking software, while marketing employees explain the deposit-return system to customers. Procurement specialists purchase materials and cleaning supplies, and senior management coordinates finance, legal compliance, and long-term planning.

Demand is increasing because European packaging regulations are becoming stricter. Retailers want alternatives that help them meet waste-reduction targets. At the same time, competitors are introducing cheaper reusable containers. FreshLoop’s main difficulty is profitability: transportation and cleaning costs are higher than expected, especially when collection volumes are low. Some managers argue that the patented seal is the company’s main source of value. Others believe that the return and cleaning network is more important because it makes repeated use possible.

FreshLoop is conducting a value-chain review before deciding where to invest. Management wants to distinguish primary activities that directly create and deliver the reusable service from support activities such as technology development, procurement, human-resource management, and firm infrastructure. The review will influence decisions about expanding cleaning capacity, improving tracking technology, outsourcing transportation, and licensing the sealing system.

Managers map the complete journey of a container, from material purchasing and manufacturing to customer use, collection, cleaning, inspection, redistribution, and support. They want employees to classify activities according to the value-chain framework rather than simply describing every visible facility as infrastructure. This distinction will help FreshLoop identify where cost reductions might damage the service and where investment could improve customer value.

FreshLoop’s original intended strategy was to sell annual subscriptions to large retailers. Pilot results showed limited consumer participation, while independent restaurants strongly preferred a deposit-return service. Regional managers responded by expanding neighborhood collection points and cleaning capacity, creating a realized strategy that differed from the original plan. The company is now considering a differentiation strategy based on container durability, convenient returns, and its patented freshness technology. A competing proposal would emphasize low price, but managers worry that cost leadership could weaken hygiene, collection coverage, and service reliability.

rcase.title: GreenCity Permits
text: GreenCity’s municipal permit department processes applications for home renovations, business signs, public events, and small construction projects. The department still relies heavily on paper files, email attachments, and in-person appointments. Residents often travel to the municipal office simply to check whether a document has been received. Employees spend considerable time searching for files and manually transferring information between systems.

Public dissatisfaction is growing. Surveys show that residents consider the process slow and difficult to understand. Average processing time has increased to seven weeks, and missing documents cause repeated delays. Local businesses argue that slow permits postpone investments. At the same time, national digital-accessibility standards will soon require municipalities to provide online services that people with different abilities can use effectively.

The department plans to introduce an online portal through which residents can submit documents, monitor progress, and receive requests for additional information. Human support will remain available by telephone and at municipal service points. Nevertheless, employees express concerns. Some fear that older residents will be excluded, while others worry that automation will make their administrative knowledge less valuable. Several supervisors prefer gradual technical improvements without changing the existing process.

The department head believes the organization first needs a shared understanding of why change is necessary. At a staff meeting, she presents waiting-time data, examples of lost documents, survey results, and direct citizen complaints. She compares GreenCity’s performance with municipalities that already provide accessible online services. She also explains the approaching national standards and the consequences of failing to meet them.

Afterward, the department forms a guiding group of employees, accessibility specialists, community representatives, and IT staff. The group develops a vision of “accessible permits anywhere, with human support when needed.” A pilot in one district later reduces processing time by 30 percent. GreenCity uses Kotter’s model to understand how urgency, a guiding coalition, a clear vision, short-term wins, and cultural reinforcement contribute to change. The immediate question is how to classify the department head’s opening use of performance evidence and public complaints.

The sequence is important. The department head does not begin by purchasing software or changing job descriptions. She first demonstrates that delay, citizen dissatisfaction, and approaching legal standards make the current situation unsustainable. The evidence is intended to overcome complacency and establish a shared reason for action before the coalition develops solutions and the pilot produces measurable results.

The later steps provide additional evidence for classification. The mixed group of employees, accessibility experts, residents, and IT specialists functions as a guiding coalition. The statement about accessible permits provides a change vision. The district pilot’s measurable 30 percent reduction in processing time is communicated as a short-term win. Leaders plan to use training, performance expectations, and continuing citizen feedback to reinforce the new process. Each action belongs to a different part of Kotter’s sequence, even though all support the same overall transformation.

rcase.title: UrbanStay Hotels
text: UrbanStay Hotels operates medium-sized properties in European business districts. Before the pandemic, most guests were employees traveling for meetings, conferences, and short assignments. UrbanStay’s mission emphasized dependable accommodation for business travelers, and its operating model was designed around high weekday occupancy. The hotels offered standard rooms, meeting spaces, breakfast, and corporate billing arrangements.

Remote and hybrid work have changed travel behavior. Many companies now hold routine meetings online, reducing traditional weekday bookings. At the same time, a different group of guests has emerged. Remote professionals, consultants, and entrepreneurs increasingly combine work and travel. They may stay for several weeks and expect reliable internet, comfortable workspaces, flexible services, and opportunities to connect with local communities.

Senior management originally intended to restore occupancy through discounted room rates for existing corporate customers. A formal plan was approved, and hotels received standard promotional materials. However, regional managers in Lisbon and Copenhagen observed that discounts did not address the needs of longer-stay guests. Without waiting for a full company-wide redesign, they tested monthly packages combining accommodation, coworking space, laundry services, and community activities.

The pilots produced unexpected results. Occupancy increased, guests stayed longer, and revenue per guest was higher than under the discount program. Customer feedback showed that the package’s convenience and social elements were more important than a low nightly price. Other regional managers began copying the approach, and UrbanStay gradually redirected marketing resources toward flexible long-stay packages.

The strategy department is reviewing what happened. The original discount program represents what senior leaders deliberately planned. The monthly package emerged through local experimentation and became a consistent pattern because it produced results. Management recognizes that an organization’s realized strategy may differ from its intended strategy when experience, learning, or external developments lead managers to adjust their actions. UrbanStay must now decide whether to formalize the monthly package across the group and revise its mission and vision accordingly.

Executives emphasize that the local packages were not isolated accidents. Managers repeated them over several months, allocated staff and space to support them, and shared the approach with other regions. The resulting pattern became more important than the original discount plan. The case therefore requires students to distinguish what leadership initially intended from what the organization ultimately implemented and learned to perform successfully.

UrbanStay’s internal review identifies centrally located properties and corporate relationships as strengths, while high energy costs and outdated meeting rooms are weaknesses. Growing demand for extended work-from-anywhere stays is an external opportunity, whereas aggressive competition from flexible-apartment platforms is a threat. Leaders are also reconsidering the organization’s future aspiration. A proposed vision describes UrbanStay as Europe’s leading home for flexible and sustainable mobile professionals, distinguishing an aspirational future from its present mission, operating activities, and legal responsibilities.

rcase.title: CareConnect Hospital
text: CareConnect Hospital has traditionally stored patient information in separate paper files maintained by different departments. Doctors, nurses, pharmacists, and laboratory employees often record related information in different locations. This creates delays when files must be transferred and increases the risk that employees will overlook important information. Hospital leaders believe that one electronic patient-record system will improve safety, reduce duplicated tests, and make information available during treatment.

The proposed change affects almost every clinical role. Doctors support faster access to laboratory results but worry that data entry will reduce the time available for patients. Nurses are concerned about using computers during busy shifts. Some experienced employees believe paper records are safer because familiar routines have worked for many years. Others welcome the opportunity to reduce repeated paperwork.

CareConnect begins with communication, training, and a supervised pilot in one department. Employees practice entering information, and technical staff remain available during every shift. The pilot reveals problems with screen design and role responsibilities, so leaders revise the workflow and provide additional coaching. These activities represent the movement toward new behavior rather than the final stage of change.

After the revised system performs reliably, CareConnect focuses on making the new approach stable. Electronic documentation becomes part of formal job descriptions. Audits measure whether required information is entered correctly, and performance discussions include appropriate system use. New employees receive training during orientation, while experienced staff receive continuing support. Senior clinicians consistently use the system during patient rounds and correct colleagues who return to unofficial paper notes.

Hospital leaders use Lewin’s three-stage model to understand the process. Unfreezing creates readiness by questioning the old system. Changing involves learning and testing the new behavior. Refreezing stabilizes the behavior by aligning structures, expectations, and routines with the change. CareConnect now wants managers to recognize which of its actions most clearly demonstrates refreezing rather than preparation or implementation.

Managers review several actions that occurred at different times. Presenting safety concerns challenged the existing approach. Training and the pilot helped employees practice unfamiliar behavior. Formal job requirements, audits, performance discussions, orientation, and visible senior-clinician behavior now make the electronic system part of normal work. These later mechanisms reduce the likelihood that departments will return to separate unofficial paper routines.

Not every employee responds in the same way. Some attend training but secretly continue using paper records when supervisors are absent, demonstrating passive rather than active resistance. The belief that paper is inherently safer is not merely a visible artifact or formal policy; for experienced staff it operates as a deeply taken-for-granted underlying assumption. Leaders therefore combine structural reinforcement with visible role modeling to change both behavior and the meaning employees attach to safe documentation.

rcase.title: NorthSea Foods
text: NorthSea Foods is a European food producer with brands in traditional dairy products, plant-based alternatives, snacks, and desserts. For many years, the company’s dairy business generated most of its revenue. More recently, NorthSea has invested in plant-based drinks, meat alternatives, and protein-rich snacks. Senior management wants the portfolio to remain profitable while responding to changes in customer expectations and regulation.

The market is developing quickly. A growing group of consumers is reducing its use of animal products because of health concerns, animal-welfare values, allergies, and environmental awareness. Supermarkets are giving more shelf space to plant-based products, and social media has made new eating patterns visible across age groups. Younger consumers often expect food companies to explain where ingredients come from and how products affect people, animals, and the environment.

Other environmental forces are also relevant. Inflation is increasing ingredient and transportation costs. New production technologies are improving the taste and texture of plant-based food. Governments are debating agricultural subsidies, while environmental labeling rules require clearer information about emissions. Climate change may affect the availability and price of crops used in both dairy and plant-based production. These developments belong to different parts of the external environment and may require different strategic responses.

NorthSea’s managers are using PESTEL to organize the information. Political factors include government priorities and agricultural policy. Economic factors include inflation, interest rates, and purchasing power. Social factors concern lifestyles, values, demographics, and consumption preferences. Technological factors include production methods and product innovation. Environmental factors concern climate and natural resources, while legal factors include mandatory standards and enforceable labeling requirements

The classification matters because managers must understand what is driving demand. If plant-based growth mainly reflects changing values and lifestyles, marketing and product development may need to respond differently than they would to a legal requirement or temporary economic condition. NorthSea therefore wants employees to distinguish the increasing consumer preference for plant-based food from the separate legal trend toward stricter environmental labeling.

Market researchers report that the preference exists even in countries without new labeling laws or additional subsidies. Interviews repeatedly mention personal health, animal welfare, identity, and environmental concern as reasons for changing diets. Management concludes that regulation may influence how products are described, but it does not fully explain why consumers are voluntarily choosing different foods and incorporating them into everyday routines.

The company also reviews its portfolio through the BCG Matrix. Traditional dairy has high market share in a slow-growth market and supplies stable cash. The plant-based brand has high share in a rapidly growing market but still needs investment. A seaweed-snack brand operates in a growing category with low share, while an older dessert brand has low share in a low-growth market. Decisions about allocating resources across these different businesses belong to corporate strategy rather than the functional or team level.

To support its strategic planning, NorthSea combines its external analysis with portfolio data. Management recognizes that identifying environmental trends is only useful when those insights influence strategic choices. The company therefore compares the market growth and relative market position of its four major businesses. Managers must decide which businesses can generate resources, which require continued investment, which need selective strategic attention, and which may have limited future potential. These decisions help NorthSea translate external analysis into corporate-level resource allocation and execution.

rcase.title: AeroLogistics
text: AeroLogistics specializes in urgent deliveries of medicines, laboratory samples, and small medical devices. Most deliveries currently travel by road. This works well in cities, but remote communities may wait several hours because of distance, traffic, ferries, or severe weather. Healthcare customers have asked AeroLogistics to investigate faster alternatives without weakening safety or reliability.

Recent advances in drone technology create a possible solution. Modern drones can carry heavier loads, navigate longer routes, and transmit detailed flight information. However, aviation regulation is still developing, and communities have concerns about noise, privacy, and safety. Several competitors are testing similar services in partnership with technology startups.

AeroLogistics forms a cross-functional innovation team that includes pilots, engineers, logistics employees, healthcare customers, safety specialists, and community representatives. The team runs a limited pilot between one pharmacy and an island clinic. The route follows all current safety requirements and reduces average delivery time from three hours to forty minutes. The company publishes the results and asks participants to identify improvements.

Management wants more employees to propose ideas for routes, packaging, scheduling, and community communication. Leaders recognize that innovation requires experimentation and that not every proposal will succeed. They establish clear boundaries: experiments must follow safety rules, use evidence, and have an agreed learning purpose. When a responsible experiment fails to meet its target, the team documents the result, explains what was learned, and decides whether to revise or discontinue the idea.

Some managers argue that unsuccessful experiments should reduce an employee’s performance rating. Others believe automatic punishment would discourage useful ideas and cause employees to hide problems. AeroLogistics therefore reviews how leadership behavior, psychological safety, cross-functional collaboration, and attitudes toward responsible failure shape an innovative culture. The company does not want uncontrolled risk-taking, but it also does not want employees to wait until competitors have proven every idea. Managers must distinguish a learning-oriented innovative culture from a culture that either punishes experimentation or ignores responsible controls.

The leadership team clarifies that learning from failure does not mean accepting carelessness. Proposals must still use evidence, respect regulations, and protect patients and communities. The cultural question concerns how the organization responds when a well-designed experiment produces an unexpected result. Leaders believe that open discussion of such outcomes can improve later decisions, whereas blame may encourage employees to hide information or avoid proposing improvements.

The case also illustrates how external developments can be classified. Advances in drone design are technological, uncertain aviation requirements are legal, competitor partnerships are competitive, and community concerns reflect changing social expectations. The island pilot provides a short-term win because it reduces delivery time while meeting safety standards. Together, the external classification, measurable result, and learning-oriented treatment of responsible experiments help managers explain why innovation can strengthen service quality and future competitive position.

As AeroLogistics considers expanding the drone service, management also examines whether the innovation can create lasting value. A Value Chain analysis shows that drone technology could improve outbound logistics by reducing delivery times, while engineering expertise, healthcare partnerships, and flight-data capabilities support the new service. A VRIO analysis suggests that the drone itself is not a unique resource because competitors can purchase similar technology. However, AeroLogistics’ combination of medical-logistics knowledge, safety expertise, healthcare relationships, and learning from pilot projects may be more difficult for competitors to reproduce. Management therefore recognizes that successful innovation depends not only on adopting new technology, but also on developing the organizational capabilities and culture needed to use it effectively.
